docs.title: Quant Trading Knowledge Base
docs.text:
How quantitative trading firms trade US equities, with strategies and algorithms first.

Last updated: 2026-11

docs.title: What this is
docs.text: This knowledge base covers what quant firms actually trade, why each strategy makes money, and who is on the other side. It then covers the concrete algorithms inside the research-and-trading pipeline: signal construction, forecasting, validation, risk models and optimization, execution, and market-making logic. The goal is a medium-deep, accurate mental model: enough to discuss any strategy family with a quant, follow an idea from signal to P&L, read short Python for the core algorithms, and tell real insight from marketing.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: A finance professional who is comfortable with valuation, accounting, capital markets and filings, has CFA-level statistics, and reads Python without being a production engineer. Finance basics are skipped. Microstructure, stat-arb math, finance-specific machine-learning pitfalls, optimization, execution theory and market-making models are taught from first principles. Intuition comes first, numbers second, and math sits in collapsible blocks.

docs.title: Start with strategies and algorithms
docs.text:
Two modules carry this knowledge base and get most of its words, labs and fact-checking. Strategies holds 30 dossiers. Algorithms holds 39 cards and 4 end-to-end walkthroughs. A good first hour:

  1. The big picture: the whole industry on one page.
  2. Strategies: the map: who makes money doing what.
  3. There is no single algorithm: five canonical pipelines, with pseudocode.
  4. One walkthrough, such as a mid-frequency stat-arb book.

docs.title: The labs
docs.text: Twenty small Python labs on synthetic data make the core algorithms concrete. They range from a matching engine and Avellaneda-Stoikov quoting to purged cross-validation, mean-variance optimization and the Almgren-Chriss frontier. Each is a single deterministic script, small enough to run on a laptop, and its plots are embedded in the relevant pages. See Labs for the list, or browse the code on GitHub.

docs.title: How to read confidence tags
docs.text:
Every number and every firm-specific claim carries a tag:

Tag Meaning Example of use [Verified] Primary source: a regulator's rule or order, an exchange document, a filing, a paper What SEC Rule 15c3-5 requires of broker-dealers with market access [Reported] Credible secondary source: reputable press, a practitioner book Press coverage of a firm's IPO filing [Estimate] Derived in this KB; the reasoning is shown next to it How long an optimizer takes to solve for 3,000 stocks [Lore] Widely repeated but unverified Industry rules of thumb

Sharpe ratios, capacity and return figures also state gross or net, the period, and the source type (academic backtest, fund disclosure or practitioner estimate). Numbers in worked examples are labeled illustrative.

docs.title: How this was built and its limitations
docs.text:
• AI-assisted. The KB was researched and written with AI assistance from public sources: papers, regulators' documents, filings, firm talks and blogs, reputable press and practitioner books. The master bibliography lists them.
  • Public sources only. Firm details come from public sources. Nothing here is inside information, and no firm's proprietary strategy is described as fact unless it is publicly documented.
  • Synthetic labs. The labs run on simulated markets. They show mechanisms, not achievable returns.
  • Dated. Market structure and regulation change. Time-sensitive facts are dated "as of 2026-11" and will go stale.
  • Not investment advice. This is educational material. Errors are possible; corrections are welcome as GitHub issues.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • "Quant trading" in US equities is at least seven different businesses that share one toolkit: electronic market makers, HFT prop shops, quant hedge funds, multi-manager quant pods, systematic factor managers, CTAs and agency execution desks.
  • Two coordinates place any of them: holding horizon (microseconds to months) and edge source (speed, liquidity provision, structural/regulatory, informational, behavioral, risk premium). Those two coordinates predict capital source, capacity, Sharpe ratio and how the strategy dies.
  • Every strategy runs the same pipeline (signal → forecast → portfolio → orders → fills → P&L); only the clock speed changes.
  • The economics are lopsided: short-horizon firms earn very large revenue on modest capital (Jane Street reportedly made $39.6B of 2025 net trading revenue [Reported]), while slow strategies run hundreds of billions at single-digit returns.
  • The question that matters most: who pays you, and why do they accept it?

Level: Core · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Three ways to slice the industry
docs.text:
A quant firm is defined less by its math than by who is on the other side of its trades. The same ridge regression can power a market maker's 50-millisecond fair value and a factor manager's monthly rebalance. So this KB sorts everything on three axes.

  1. Firm type: business model and capital source. A principal trading firm (PTF) risks only its own capital. A hedge fund risks investors' money for fees. An agency desk risks almost nothing and charges commissions.
  2. Holding horizon: how long a position lives. Rough bands: microseconds to seconds (HFT and market making), minutes to days (statistical arbitrage), days to weeks (mid-frequency alpha), weeks to months (factors, trend).
  3. Edge source: why the trade should make money at all. The six-way taxonomy (speed · liquidity provision · structural/regulatory · informational · behavioral · risk premium) is explained in How quants evaluate a strategy.

The chart below places firm types on horizon (log scale, left to right) against how they get paid: for a service (immediacy, execution), or for being right (a forecast) and bearing risk (a premium).

    quadrant-1 Risk premia and slow alpha

    quadrant-3 Liquidity and speed
    quadrant-4 Execution as a service
    Equity and ETF market makers: [0.10, 0.15]
    Options market makers: [0.24, 0.32]

docs.title: One pipeline, many clock speeds
docs.text:
Ask a quant "what's your algorithm?" and you will get a polite sigh: there is no single algorithm. Every firm runs the same chain of stages, each with its own algorithms. That chain is the backbone of module 03.

flowchart LR
    D["Data<br/>prices, books, fundamentals, alt data"] --> S["Signals<br/>features and alphas"]
    S --> F["Forecast<br/>expected return or fair value"]
    F --> P["Portfolio<br/>risk model, optimizer, sizing"]
    P --> O["Orders<br/>execution algos, routing"]
    O --> X["Fills<br/>venues and counterparties"]
    X --> L["PnL<br/>attribution, decay checks"]
    L -.->|"feedback"| S
Stage What happens Where to read Signal Clean point-in-time data, build features, rank and neutralize D1 · D3 · D4 Forecast Combine signals into an expected return (or a fair value) F1 · F5 · M2 Portfolio Trade forecasts off against risk and cost P1 · P3 · P5 Orders and fills Slice, schedule and route; quote and hedge for market makers E1 · E4 · M4 P&L Attribute, monitor, retire decaying models L1 · L2

For a market maker the whole loop runs in microseconds and "portfolio" collapses into inventory skew (M1). For a factor manager it runs monthly and the optimizer dominates. The algorithm map places all 39 cards on this chain.

docs.title: Where the money comes from
docs.text:
Every dollar of quant P&L is somebody's cost or somebody's risk premium. Grossman and Miller's classic model frames the first case: impatient traders pay liquidity providers for immediacy [Verified]. The pools below are rough, mixed in scope and dated; treat them as orders of magnitude.

Pool Who pays, and why they accept it Who earns it Rough scale Spread and immediacy Retail, institutions and other algos pay half-spreads and impact to trade now Market makers, PTFs Non-bank liquidity providers earned ~\(25.6B of market-making revenue in 2024, global and all asset classes [Reported]; their total revenue pool hit ~\)114B in 2025, of which pure market making was only ~30% [Reported] Speed races Slow quoters whose stale quotes get sniped, and ultimately investors through wider spreads HFT ~$5B a year in global equities, roughly a 0.5 bp tax on trading (academic estimate from UK exchange data) [Reported] Retail flow access Wholesalers pay brokers for low-toxicity retail orders, then improve on the NBBO Wholesalers, net of payments Citadel Securities paid ~$943M for retail equity and options flow, Apr–Dec 2024 (Rule 606 data) [Reported] Execution service Institutions pay commissions to have orders worked Agency brokers US equity commission wallet just under $7B in 2025, up from a $5.4B low in 2023 (survey) [Reported] Forecasting alpha Slower or constrained investors trade at predictably wrong prices Quant hedge funds, pods Hedge fund industry capital ~\(5.15T at end-2025 [Reported]; the largest quant managers ran ~\)46–78B each in mid-2025, depending on AUM definition [Reported] Risk premia Investors pay to shed risks they dislike (crashes, distress, leverage constraints) Factor managers, CTAs, vol sellers Managed-futures assets ~$365B in Q4 2025 [Reported]

Firm-level anchors for 2025: Jane Street ~\(39.6B of net trading revenue (helped by gains on private stakes), Hudson River Trading ~\)12.3B and Citadel Securities ~$12.2B, all from unnamed sources [Reported]. Virtu's adjusted net trading income was $2.15B, of which market making was $1.67B [Verified]. These are global, multi-asset figures; none of these firms discloses a US-equities-only number. History shows how fast a pool can compress: Tabb Group estimated US-equity HFT revenue fell from \(7.2B in 2009 to ~\)1.1B in 2016 [Reported]. Options volume, by contrast, set a sixth straight record in 2025: 15.26B contracts cleared, up 24% [Verified].

The structural lesson [Estimate] (reasoning: the pools above): liquidity and speed businesses earn tens of billions on balance sheets of a few billion each, because they recycle capital many times a day. Forecasting and premia businesses earn single-digit to low-teens percent on hundreds of billions. That asymmetry explains a lot: why the biggest market makers rarely take outside money, why factor managers compete on fees, and why pods pay up for PMs with genuine short-horizon alpha.

docs.title: How to use this KB
docs.text:
• Pick a path. Learning paths offers a 90-minute sprint, a 4-hour Core Path and a 2-week deep path. The cheat sheet fits on one page.
  • Spend most of your time in the two priority modules. Strategies has 30 dossiers on one map; start with How quants evaluate a strategy. Algorithms has 39 cards and four end-to-end walkthroughs; start with There is no single algorithm.
  • Run a lab when a page links one (labs index); each uses synthetic data and runs in about a minute.
  • Before a meeting, read the conversation playbook and myths vs reality.
  • Read the tags. [Verified] means a primary source; [Reported] credible press or survey; [Estimate] our derivation, with reasoning; [Lore] widely repeated, unverified. Market-structure prerequisites are in module 01.

docs.title: ETF, futures and options linkages
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • An ETF, its stock basket, the index future and index options are different wrappers on one exposure. Arbitrage keeps them within a few basis points of each other and passes flow from one to the next.
  • ETF ↔ basket: authorized participants create and redeem shares in kind. The no-arbitrage band is the cost of trading the basket plus creation fees.
  • Futures ↔ cash: fair value is spot times carry (financing minus dividends). The E-mini usually leads price discovery.
  • Options ↔ stock: put-call parity ties calls to puts, and dealers' delta hedging pushes options flow into the underlying. 0DTE reached a record 66.2% of SPX options volume in July 2026 [Verified]. Whether its hedging amplifies or dampens intraday moves is still contested.

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: One exposure, four wrappers
docs.text:
The S&P 500 can be held as 500 stocks, as an ETF such as SPY, as an E-mini future (ES), or synthetically through SPX or SPY options. Each wrapper has its own venue, costs, hours and investors. All four pay off on the same index, so a gap between them wider than trading costs is a near-riskless trade, and the fastest, cheapest firms close it. A large buy in one wrapper is quickly felt in the other three.

flowchart LR
    ETF["ETF shares<br/>(e.g. SPY)"] <-->|"create / redeem<br/>(authorized participants)"| BSK["Stock basket<br/>(500 names)"]
    BSK <-->|"cash-and-carry<br/>(basis = carry)"| FUT["Index future<br/>(ES)"]
    FUT <-->|"hedge substitute<br/>(futures usually lead)"| ETF
    OPT["Index and ETF options<br/>(SPX, SPY)"] -->|"dealer delta hedging"| FUT
    OPT -->|"dealer delta hedging"| ETF

docs.title: ETFs: creation, redemption and the arbitrage band
docs.text:
An authorized participant (AP) is a broker-dealer with a contract with the fund. To create, it delivers the fund's published basket plus a small cash component and receives a creation unit of new ETF shares. To redeem, it does the reverse. US equity ETFs mostly work in kind, which lets the fund shed low-basis shares without realizing capital gains. Cash creations, common for hard-to-trade assets, make the fund trade the securities itself and pass the cost back through a variable fee. SEC Rule 6c-11 (2019) allows custom baskets. It requires daily publication of holdings and disclosure of any premium or discount above 2% that lasts more than seven consecutive trading days [Verified].

NAV is struck once a day from closing prices. The intraday indicative value (iNAV) is a slow public estimate, and Rule 6c-11 itself does not require it [Verified]. Professional desks compute their own fair value in real time from the basket, futures and correlated ETFs (see fair value and microprice).

Worked example (illustrative). The basket is worth $100.00 per ETF share. One creation unit is 50,000 shares, or $5.0M. Trading the basket costs about 3 bp and the creation fee is $500, about 1 bp. Arbitrage therefore starts once the premium or discount exceeds about ±4 bp. Suppose the ETF bid is $100.06, a 6 bp premium. The AP sells 50,000 ETF shares for $5,003,000, buys the basket for $5,000,000, pays $1,500 in trading costs and $500 to create, and delivers. Profit is $1,000, or 2 bp. In practice an ETF market maker rarely creates per trade. It hedges with futures or the basket, nets inventory through the day and creates or redeems at the close.

sequenceDiagram
    participant AP as Authorized participant
    participant MKT as Stock market
    participant FUND as ETF issuer
    participant EXCH as ETF secondary market
    AP->>EXCH: Sell ETF shares at a premium
    AP->>MKT: Buy the creation basket
    AP->>FUND: Deliver basket plus cash component
    FUND->>AP: Issue a creation unit of new ETF shares
    AP->>EXCH: Deliver ETF shares to cover the sale

docs.title: Index futures: fair value and basis
docs.text:
The E-mini S&P 500 pays $50 times the index, expires quarterly and settles in cash. It trades nearly 23 hours a day on CME Globex [Verified]. Holding the basket costs financing and earns dividends, so the no-arbitrage futures price is

\[ F = S \, e^{(r - q)T}, \]

and the basis \(F - S\) is the net carry. With \(S\) = 6,000, financing \(r\) = 4.30%, dividend yield \(q\) = 1.30% and \(T\) = 0.25, fair value is 6,045.2 (illustrative). Suppose ES trades at 6,052. Desks restate that gap as the implied financing rate: about 4.75%, or 45 bp over the 4.30% financing rate [Estimate]. The futures are rich. An arbitrageur sells futures and buys the basket. Ten contracts capture 6.8 points × $50 × 10 = $3,400, before roughly \(600–\)1,200 of basket trading costs. The implied financing spread moves with demand for leveraged long exposure and with dealers' balance-sheet costs. That makes it a traded quantity in its own right, not a constant [Lore].

docs.title: Who leads: price discovery between futures and cash
docs.text:
Futures usually move first. One contract carries the whole index, needs low margin and has no short-sale restrictions. Hasbrouck (2003) found that the E-mini dominated price discovery for the S&P 500 [Reported]. At the millisecond scale, Budish, Cramton and Shim (2015) showed that the ES-SPY correlation breaks down. They also found that the median life of an ES-SPY arbitrage opportunity fell from 97 ms in 2005 to 7 ms in 2011 [Reported]. That race is what latency arbitrage competes in.

Leadership is not absolute. On stock-specific news, the stock leads and the index follows. In the closing auction, the cash market sets the print. Overnight, futures are the only liquid venue, so the cash open catches up to them. That last asymmetry would shrink if 23-hour exchange trading in stocks launches as planned on Dec 6, 2026 (see recent changes).

docs.title: Options: parity, delta hedging and the 0DTE debate
docs.text:
Put-call parity for European options (such as SPX) is

\[ C - P = S e^{-qT} - K e^{-rT}. \]

Violations are arbitraged through the stock or the future. In single stocks, a persistent violation usually means the shares are expensive to borrow. A synthetic short (long put, short call) becomes the cheaper way to be short, so puts trade rich. Option prices therefore reveal the borrow fee (see shorting, financing and settlement).

Delta hedging is the second channel. Market makers neutralize delta in the underlying or the future, and gamma makes that hedge trade along with the market. A dealer who is net short gamma buys as prices rise and sells as they fall, which amplifies moves. A dealer who is net long gamma does the opposite, which dampens them.

Here is a first-order illustrative example. With 3 hours left, an at-the-money SPX 0DTE option at 15% volatility has a gamma of about 0.0104 per index point. Take a dealer net short 2,000 contracts. After a 1% move of 60 points, it must trade about $750M of index exposure, roughly 2,500 ES contracts.

0DTE options were a record 66.2% of SPX volume in July 2026 [Verified]. Same-day index options averaged about 3.4M contracts a day in Q3 2026 [Reported]. The evidence on their effect cuts both ways:

View Evidence 0DTE amplifies volatility Brogaard, Han and Won estimate that a one-standard-deviation rise in 0DTE volume goes with about 14% higher daily S&P 500 volatility [Reported] 0DTE dampens or is neutral Dim, Eraker and Vilkov (2024) find that higher dealer open-interest gamma goes with lower intraday realized volatility, with no spillover to later periods [Reported]. Adams et al. argue that dealer hedging is mostly dampening [Reported]

The sign depends on net dealer positioning, which nobody observes directly. Neither view has won.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• ETF and index arbitrage and ETF market making are the creation band and the basis turned into businesses.
  • Lead-lag and cross-asset arbitrage and latency arbitrage trade the futures-lead structure.
  • Options market making, the volatility risk premium and vol arb, and dispersion and correlation trading depend on parity and hedging flows.
  • Flow-driven strategies trade around predictable ETF and index flows.
  • Algorithms:
    • Fair value and microprice builds the real-time basket value.
    • Hedging algorithms choose between futures, ETF and basket.
    • Options pricing and vol surfaces uses parity-implied forwards and borrow.
    • Order-book and trade-flow signals uses futures moves as a leading feature.

docs.title: Fees, rebates and ticks
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Maker-taker exchanges pay the resting order up to about 0.29¢ a share and charge the taker up to the 0.30¢ cap. Inverted venues do the reverse. Fee-adjusted, the real price grid is finer than the penny.
  • In tick-constrained stocks, liquidity competes on queue position, not price. There the rebate can be a third or more of a market maker's gross margin.
  • The SEC's 2024 package (half-penny tick, 0.10¢ fee cap, round lots by price tier) is only partly live. Round lots took effect Nov 3, 2025. The tick and fee-cap changes are deferred to Nov 1, 2027 and under review (as of 2026-11).
  • Rule 612 bans sub-penny quotes at $1 and above, not sub-penny executions.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Why exchanges pay you to trade
docs.text:
A maker posts a resting limit order. A taker removes it with a marketable order. Under maker-taker pricing, the exchange charges the taker an access fee, passes most of it to the maker as a rebate and keeps the rest. Inverted (taker-maker) venues charge the maker and pay the taker.

Model Maker Taker Published example (stocks ≥ $1) Maker-taker earns tiered rebate pays fee, capped at $0.0030 Nasdaq: top displayed-add rebates \(0.0029–\)0.00295; remove fee $0.0030 [Verified] Inverted pays fee earns small rebate Cboe BYX: add fee $0.0020 (tiers to $0.0013); remove rebate $0.0002 [Verified] Flat / most ATSs small fee or none small fee varies by venue

The economic price is the quoted price adjusted for the fee. Lifting a $50.00 offer costs $50.0030 all-in on a maker-taker venue. On an inverted venue it costs about $49.9998. A bid resting at $49.99 on the inverted venue really pays $49.992, which is 0.2¢ better than its quote without any sub-penny quoting. So takers sweep inverted venues first, and makers who pay to post there are buying a place at the front of the queue. A smart order router therefore ranks venues by fee-adjusted price and fill probability, not by the displayed price.

flowchart LR
    subgraph MT["Maker-taker venue"]
        T1["Taker pays 0.30 cents"] --> X1["Exchange keeps about 0.01 cents"]
        X1 --> M1["Maker earns about 0.29 cents"]
    end
    subgraph INV["Inverted venue"]
        M2["Maker pays 0.13-0.20 cents"] --> X2["Exchange keeps the difference"]
        X2 --> T2["Taker earns about 0.02 cents"]
    end
    MT --> R["Router compares fee-adjusted prices<br/>and fill odds across venues"]
    INV --> R

docs.title: Ticks, tick-constrained stocks and queues
docs.text:
Rule 612, the sub-penny rule, bars displaying, ranking or accepting orders in increments finer than $0.01 for stocks priced at $1.00 or more. Below $1 the increment is $0.0001 [Verified]. Executions are not covered: midpoint pegs fill at half-pennies, and wholesalers give retail orders fractions of a cent of improvement (see venues and retail flow).

What matters is the tick size relative to price. One cent is 10 bp of a $10 stock and 0.2 bp of a $500 stock. A stock is tick-constrained when the spread market makers would quote if they could is narrower than one tick. These are usually low-priced, low-volatility, heavily traded names. In them:

  1. The spread stays pinned at one tick. Improving the price would cross the other side.
  2. Displayed depth piles up. With 400,000 shares at the bid and 25,000 shares a minute trading there, a newly joined order waits about 16 minutes (illustrative).
  3. Time priority becomes the asset. Orders at the front fill on ordinary flow. Orders at the back fill mainly when an informed trader clears the whole level, so they bear more adverse selection. That is why queue position has a measurable value.
flowchart TD
    A["Natural spread vs one tick"] -->|"narrower than 1 tick"| B["Tick-constrained<br/>spread pinned at 1 tick"]
    A -->|"several ticks wide"| C["Spread free to move"]
    B --> D["Long queues. Competition on<br/>time priority, fees and venue choice"]
    C --> E["Competition on price.<br/>Quotes step inside the spread"]
    D --> F["Key models: queue value,<br/>fee-adjusted routing, markouts"]
    E --> G["Key models: fair value,<br/>spread and skew setting"]

Round and odd lots. Only round lots count toward the protected NBBO. At 100 shares for every stock, a round lot of a $900 stock was $90,000, so better-priced odd-lot orders often sat invisibly inside the NBBO. Since Nov 3, 2025, the round lot depends on the stock's average closing price in the prior evaluation month, with reassignment twice a year [Verified]:

Average closing price Round lot up to $250.00 100 shares \(250.01–\)1,000.00 40 shares \(1,000.01–\)10,000.00 10 shares above $10,000 1 share

Since late April 2026 the SIPs have also disseminated the best odd-lot order. Odd-lot depth between that order and the NBBO is deferred to May 2028 [Verified]. Details are in NBBO and market data.

docs.title: The 2024 amendments (status as of 2026-11)
docs.text:
The SEC adopted the package on Sep 18, 2024 [Verified]. It had two parts that change unit economics:

  • Half-penny tick. Stocks priced at $1 or more with a time-weighted average quoted spread of $0.015 or less over an evaluation period would quote in $0.005 increments. All others keep $0.01 [Verified].
  • Access-fee cap. The cap falls from $0.0030 to $0.0010 per share for stocks priced at $1 or more [Verified]. Rebates are funded by take fees, so they must fall too.

Compliance was first due Nov 3, 2025. An Oct 31, 2025 order moved it to Nov 2, 2026. A June 2026 order moved it to Nov 1, 2027 and came alongside a staff review of both rules [Reported]. Treat both parts as unsettled. Recent changes tracks the dates.

docs.title: Worked example: a market maker's per-share P&L
docs.text:
Take a passive market maker quoting both sides of a tick-constrained $40 stock with a 1¢ spread. It earns top-tier rebates and exits 20% of its inventory aggressively. All figures are per share filled and illustrative.

P&L line (per share) Today: 1¢ tick, $0.0030 cap If the 2024 rules applied Half-spread captured +$0.0050 +$0.0025 Maker rebate +$0.0029 +$0.0008 [Estimate], the cap minus exchange margin Adverse selection (markout to mid) −$0.0045 −$0.0030 [Estimate], falls less than the spread Aggressive exits: 20% × (half-spread + take fee) −$0.0016 −$0.0007 Clearing and regulatory fees −$0.0002 −$0.0002 Net +$0.0016 −$0.0006

Read it as an income statement. The rebate is 37% of today's $0.0079 gross revenue, and without it the book loses $0.0013 a share. If the 2024 rules took effect, both the tick rent and the rebate would shrink. Survival would then depend on better markouts, which means better short-horizon prediction, or on more volume per quote [Estimate].

docs.title: Rebate capture: the logic and its limits
docs.text:
Rebate capture means routing and timing trades so you collect rebates instead of paying fees. Moving one share from taking (−0.30¢) to making (+0.29¢) is worth about 0.6¢. For a stat-arb book trading 5 million shares a day, that is about $30,000 a day, or $7.5M a year (illustrative). Three limits:

  • Selection and non-fills. Passive orders fill most often just before the price moves through them. Orders that never fill need a costlier catch-up trade later. Rebate capture only pays when the alpha horizon is long relative to the queue wait.
  • Tiers reward scale. Top rebates need a set share of consolidated volume each month, so large firms concentrate flow to hit the tier. A 2023 SEC proposal to curb volume tiers was withdrawn on Jun 12, 2025 [Reported].
  • Agency conflict. Brokers that route client limit orders to the venue with the highest rebate keep the rebate, and their clients get worse fills. Battalio, Corwin and Jennings (2016) documented this [Reported].

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Market making. Equity market making and ETF market making earn half-spread plus rebate minus markout. The table above is their P&L skeleton.
  • Fee-driven strategies. Fee- and microstructure-driven strategies trade on fee-adjusted prices and queue dynamics directly.
  • High-turnover books. For short-term reversal, the 0.6¢ make-or-take swing decides whether the strategy is profitable.
  • Algorithms. Fees and ticks are explicit inputs to:
    • queue position and order placement;
    • quoting and inventory control;
    • adverse selection and markouts;
    • smart order routing;
    • transaction cost and impact models.

docs.title: Life of a stock order
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A US stock order travels one of two very different pipes. Retail marketable orders mostly go from the broker to a handful of wholesalers that fill them off-exchange. Institutional orders go to an execution algorithm whose smart order router slices them across 18 exchanges, 33 ATSs and the closing auction.
  • Every hop gets paid: payment for order flow, spread capture, access fees and rebates, commissions, clearing fees. Follow the money and you find the strategies in module 02.
  • After the fill, the trade prints to the tape (exchange or FINRA TRF). NSCC becomes the central counterparty and nets it, and DTC settles it one business day later (T+1).
  • Latency spans about ten orders of magnitude: microseconds for colocated hops, milliseconds for a retail app, hours for an algo's schedule, a day for settlement.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Two pipes, one tape
docs.text:
A retail investor's 50-share market order and a pension fund's 2-million-share parent order both end up as prints on the consolidated tape and positions at DTC. In between, they touch different intermediaries, at different speeds, with different people on the other side.

flowchart LR
    R1["Retail investor app"] --> B1["Retail broker"]
    B1 -->|"marketable orders"| W1["Wholesaler (internalizer)"]
    B1 -->|"some limit orders"| X1["Exchanges (lit)"]
    W1 -->|"hedges and residuals"| X1
    I1["Portfolio manager"] --> O1["OMS"]
    O1 --> A1["Execution algo (VWAP, IS)"]
    A1 --> S1["Smart order router"]
    S1 --> X1
    S1 --> D1["ATSs and dark pools"]
    S1 --> C1["Closing auction"]
    W1 --> T1["FINRA TRF print"]
    D1 --> T1
    X1 --> T2["Exchange print"]
    C1 --> T2
    T1 --> N1["NSCC: novate and net"]
    T2 --> N1
    N1 --> S2["DTC: settle on T+1"]

docs.title: The retail pipe
docs.text:
1. Broker. The investor taps "buy". After risk checks, the broker's routing table sends marketable orders (market orders, and limits priced at or through the far side of the NBBO) to wholesalers. When the SEC proposed its Order Competition Rule in December 2022, it found that brokers routed more than 90% of individual investors' marketable orders to six off-exchange dealers [Verified]. Zero-commission brokers earn payment for order flow (PFOF), interest on client cash and margin-lending spread instead.
  2. Wholesaler. The wholesaler fills the order as principal at or better than the NBBO. It usually hands back part of the spread as price improvement. This is internalization. Robinhood's 2025 Rule 606 reports list Citadel Securities, Virtu and Jane Street among its paying venues [Verified]. It can improve the price and still pay the broker because retail flow carries little short-term information (Venues and retail flow explains why). Unwanted orders and accumulated inventory go to exchanges.
  3. Print. The fill is reported to a FINRA trade reporting facility (TRF) and appears on the tape as an off-exchange trade. Off-exchange volume reached 50.6% of consolidated volume in 2025, the first year above half. Principal dealers, mostly wholesalers, accounted for 81% of that [Verified].

docs.title: The institutional pipe
docs.text:
1. Decision to order. A portfolio manager's rebalance becomes an order in the OMS, for example "buy 2M XYZ today, implementation-shortfall benchmark".
  2. Algo. An in-house or broker algorithm (VWAP, POV, implementation shortfall) cuts the parent into thousands of child orders over minutes to the full session. The point is to limit market impact.
  3. Router. For each child, the smart order router picks a venue and an order type. It can post passively on an exchange and wait in the queue, or ping dark pools with midpoint IOCs. It can sweep several lit venues at once with ISOs, or send market-on-close orders to the auction.
  4. Feedback. Fills stream back, the algo re-plans, and transaction cost analysis (TCA) scores the result afterwards.

The other side of those child orders is whoever is resting in the book: market makers, other algos, and occasionally another institution in a block-crossing ATS.

docs.title: Clearing and settlement
docs.text:
Once a trade is matched, the exchange or TRF sends locked-in trade details to NSCC, a DTCC subsidiary. NSCC is the central counterparty: through novation it becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer. If a member defaults, NSCC stands behind the trade. Its continuous net settlement system nets each member's buys and sells in each security down to one delivery or receipt. Members post clearing-fund margin sized to their unsettled exposure. On settlement date, DTC moves the shares against cash. US equities settle T+1, one business day after trade date, the standard since May 2024 [Reported]. Most funds face NSCC through a clearing or prime broker, which charges fees and sets margin and stock-loan terms.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as Retail app
    participant BD as Retail broker
    participant WS as Wholesaler
    participant EX as Exchange
    participant TRF as FINRA TRF
    participant CCP as NSCC
    participant DTC as DTC
    App->>BD: Buy 100 XYZ at market
    BD->>WS: Route marketable order under PFOF terms
    WS->>WS: Price against NBBO and decide to internalize
    WS-->>BD: Fill at NBO minus price improvement
    BD-->>App: Execution confirmation
    WS->>TRF: Report the trade to the tape
    WS->>EX: Later, hedge or offload inventory
    TRF->>CCP: Locked-in trade details
    CCP->>CCP: Novate and net by security
    CCP->>DTC: Net settlement instructions
    DTC-->>BD: Shares and cash move on T+1

docs.text: Intermediary What it does How it is paid Order of magnitude Retail broker App, custody, routing PFOF, interest on cash and margin; commission usually zero Tens of cents to about $1 per 100 shares in 2025 Rule 606 reports [Reported] Wholesaler Fills retail as principal Spread captured, minus price improvement, minus PFOF Citadel Securities paid about $341M for US retail equity and options flow in Q2 2025 [Reported] Institutional broker Algos, router, capital Commission per share Roughly 0.5–2 cents/share for execution-only algos [Lore] Exchange Matching, protected quotes Taker (access) fees, market data and connectivity; pays maker rebates Access-fee cap 30 mils ($0.0030/share), 10 mils once the 2024 amendment takes effect [Verified] ATS / dark pool Non-displayed matching Per-share fees About 19% of TRF volume in 2025 [Verified] NSCC and DTC Clearing, netting, settlement Per-trade fees; clearing-fund margin Fees tiny; margin is the real cost [Lore] Clearing broker Access to NSCC, financing Clearing fees, financing spread, stock-loan fees See shorting and settlement

docs.title: The latency scale
docs.text:
Hop Typical latency Tag and reasoning Retail app to broker over the internet 10–100 ms [Estimate] consumer-internet round trip Broker to wholesaler and back about 1 ms or less [Estimate] dedicated lines between New Jersey data centers Wholesaler pricing decision microseconds to about 1 ms [Lore] Portfolio manager decision to first child order minutes to hours [Lore] human workflow Life of an algo parent order minutes to a full session [Lore] slow on purpose, to cut impact Router to an exchange, colocated about 5–50 μs one way [Estimate] tens of meters of fiber plus switch and gateway Between data centers in Mahwah, Carteret and Secaucus about 90–190 μs one way [Estimate] 27–56 km at 3.34 μs/km by microwave; about 1.5× slower over fiber Trade to settlement 1 business day T+1 [Reported]

From about 10 μs to one day (roughly 1011 μs) is ten orders of magnitude [Estimate]; each band supports its own kind of strategy.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• The retail pipe is a business. Wholesalers run retail flow internalization. Its edge is the low toxicity of the flow, measured with markouts.
  • The institutional pipe is the execution stack. The parent-to-child cascade is covered in Execution algorithms overview, VWAP, TWAP and POV, Smart order routing and Transaction cost analysis. Walkthrough: executing a $500M buy order tells the whole story with numbers.
  • The child orders are someone's revenue. Equity market making quotes against them. Auctions and closing liquidity is about the end-of-day share of them.
  • The latency table is a cost structure. Latency arbitrage and the HFT trading loop live in the microsecond rows. Mid-frequency books such as factor-residual mean reversion live in the minutes-to-hours rows and pay for settlement, borrow and financing.

docs.title: NBBO and market data
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The NBBO is the best displayed round-lot bid and offer across all exchanges. The SIPs compute it centrally, and every serious trader also computes it themselves from direct exchange feeds.
  • Direct feeds beat the SIP by roughly 0.2–0.5 ms, mostly because of geography and an extra hop, not slow processing. That gap is the raw material of latency arbitrage.
  • The SIP carries top-of-book and trades. Direct feeds carry full depth, often order by order, which you need to track queue position.
  • The 2020 Market Data Infrastructure rule is only partly in force: price-tiered round lots went live on November 3, 2025 and odd-lot top-of-book was scheduled for the SIP from May 2026. Odd-lot depth is deferred to May 2028, and competing consolidators are not yet operating.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Intuition: one price, many copies
docs.text: Eighteen exchanges each publish their own best bid and offer. The NBBO (national best bid and offer) is the highest bid and lowest offer among them, as computed by whoever is looking, from whatever data has reached them. Two traders can see different NBBOs at the same instant; the slower one is trading on a stale price.

docs.title: What counts, and what the NBBO is used for
docs.text:
Only protected quotes count: automated, displayed, round-lot quotes on exchanges. Hidden orders, odd lots and off-exchange liquidity do not set the NBBO, even when they offer better prices. The NBBO then serves as the yardstick for:

  • the trade-through rule (Rule 611), which bars executions at prices worse than a protected quote. Its rescission was proposed in June 2026 [Verified].
  • price improvement and Rule 605 statistics.
  • midpoint pegs and most dark-pool pricing.
  • wholesaler fills to retail.

Round lots changed on November 3, 2025. The round lot is now 100 shares for stocks up to $250, 40 shares from $250.01 to $1,000, 10 shares from $1,000.01 to $10,000, and 1 share above that [Verified]. Nasdaq estimated that over 200 stocks were affected [Reported]. Illustration: in a $900 stock, the best 100-share quotes might be $899.80 × $900.20 while 40-share orders sit at $899.95 × $900.05, so the official NBBO narrows from 40 cents to 10.

Odd-lot data comes next. The SIPs were scheduled to begin carrying each exchange's best odd-lot quote at or better than the NBBO, plus a consolidated best odd-lot order (BOLO), from late April and May 2026 [Verified]. TODO(verify): confirm the go-live happened as scheduled. Odd-lot quotes are not protected and can lock or cross the NBBO [Verified]. A January 2026 SEC exemptive order deferred odd-lot depth of book to May 2028 [Verified].

docs.title: SIP vs direct feeds
docs.text:
SIP (consolidated tape) Direct feeds (proprietary) Who runs it CTA/CQ plans for NYSE- and other-listed stocks (processor in Mahwah); UTP plan for Nasdaq-listed stocks (processor in Carteret) [Reported] Each exchange, for its own book Content Top of book per exchange, NBBO, trades (including TRF prints), limit-up/limit-down bands, odd-lot top of book from 2026 Full depth of book, often order by order, plus auction imbalance feeds Processing latency Fell from milliseconds (0.38 ms for Tape A/B quotes in 4Q2013) to microseconds today [Verified]; about tens of μs on average [Lore] Generated inside the exchange's data center End-to-end disadvantage About 0.2–0.5 ms behind a colocated direct-feed reader [Estimate], derived below — Users Retail displays, best-execution benchmarks, many buy-side systems Market makers, HFT, broker routers, sophisticated dark pools

Why the SIP is slower: a numeric sketch [Estimate]. Suppose an NYSE Arca quote changes in Mahwah for a Nasdaq-listed stock, and a trader is colocated in Carteret, about 56 km away.

  • Direct: the Arca feed goes over microwave at about 3.34 μs/km, so it arrives in about 190 μs.
  • SIP: the same quote travels by fiber to the UTP processor in Carteret. Assume a route 1.3× the straight line at about 4.9 μs/km, so about 360 μs. Add tens of μs of processing, and the update arrives about 400 μs after the event.

The gap is about 200 μs; for a trader in Secaucus, who must wait for the SIP output to travel back from Carteret, it is closer to 400–450 μs. A faster SIP computer would not close it: geography and the extra hop dominate.

flowchart LR
    M1["NYSE group engines<br/>Mahwah"] -->|"direct feed, microwave"| HF["Colocated trader<br/>own NBBO"]
    C1["Nasdaq engines<br/>Carteret"] -->|"direct feed"| HF
    S1["Cboe and others<br/>Secaucus"] -->|"direct feed"| HF
    M1 -->|"fiber"| SP["SIP processors<br/>CTA in Mahwah, UTP in Carteret"]
    C1 --> SP
    S1 -->|"fiber"| SP
    SP -->|"consolidated NBBO, later"| US["Retail brokers, benchmarks,<br/>SIP-priced pegs"]

docs.title: Why "the SIP is slower" matters: stale quotes
docs.text:
Here is an illustrative race. The NBBO is $20.00 × $20.01 everywhere. A large seller sweeps every $20.00 bid, so the true market is now about $19.99 × $20.00. A dark pool that prices its midpoint pegs off the SIP still shows $20.005 for a few hundred microseconds. A trader on direct feeds sells to the resting midpoint buyer at $20.005 and buys back around $19.995 once market makers re-quote. That is about 1 cent per share, paid by the slow peg. This is latency arbitrage in its purest form.

sequenceDiagram
    participant EX as Exchanges
    participant HF as Fast trader
    participant SIP as SIP
    participant DP as Dark pool peg
    EX->>HF: Bids at 20.00 swept, direct feed after about 0.1 ms
    HF->>DP: Sell at stale mid 20.005, about 0.2 ms
    DP-->>HF: Fill against resting midpoint buyer
    EX->>SIP: Same update still in transit
    SIP->>DP: New NBBO arrives after about 0.4 ms
    DP->>DP: Peg reprices to 19.995, too late
    Note over HF,DP: About 1 cent per share moves from the slow peg to the fast trader

How big is it? Using exchange message data for London's FTSE 100 stocks, Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill (2022) found latency-arbitrage races in about 20% of trading volume. They work out a cost equal to roughly a 0.5 bp tax on trading, about $5B a year across global equity markets [Verified]. Bartlett and McCrary, by contrast, argued that arbitrage against the US SIP specifically was too small after 2015 to explain the arms race [Reported], and many venues now price off direct feeds [Lore]. The evidence is mixed.

docs.title: The Market Data Infrastructure rule: status
docs.text:
Adopted in December 2020, the MDI rule had two parts [Verified]:

  1. It expands "core data" to include some depth of book, auction information, odd-lot quotes and a price-based round lot.
  2. It replaces the exclusive SIPs with competing private consolidators and self-aggregators.

The D.C. Circuit upheld it in 2022 [Reported]. Progress since:

  • The round-lot and odd-lot pieces were pulled forward by the September 2024 Regulation NMS amendments and are now live or scheduled [Verified].
  • The consolidator half has stalled. A new consolidated-data (CT) Plan is meant to replace the three legacy plans. As of April 2026 its fee schedule was still in SEC proceedings, and the CTA, CQ and UTP plans still governed SIP data [Verified].
  • TODO(verify): confirm that no competing consolidator has begun operating.
timeline
    title US market data reform
    2020-12 : Market Data Infrastructure rule adopted
    2022 : D.C. Circuit upholds the rule
    2024-09 : Round lot and odd-lot pieces pulled forward
    2025-11 : Price-tiered round lots live
    2026-01 : Odd-lot depth on the SIP deferred to 2028
    2026-05 : Odd-lot top of book and BOLO scheduled on the SIP
    2026-06 : Rescission of the trade-through rule proposed

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• The gap is a strategy. Latency arbitrage and lead-lag and cross-asset arbitrage monetize it. The HFT trading loop is built to stay on the right side of it.
  • Market makers need direct, deep data. Equity market making and ETF market making quote from their own NBBO. They use depth for the microprice and order-book signals, and order-by-order data for queue position.
  • Benchmarks depend on the feed. Price improvement in retail flow internalization and slippage in transaction cost analysis are measured against an NBBO. Which NBBO, and at which timestamp, changes the answer.
  • Backtests inherit the feed's flaws. SIP-timestamped data understates how stale quotes were. See point-in-time data and cleaning and backtesting engines.

docs.title: Order types and auctions
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • An order type is a contract with the matching engine: which price, how long, whether you may take liquidity, and what happens to the rest. Quants use only a handful of them: limit, IOC, ISO, post-only, midpoint peg and the on-close family.
  • ISOs let a router hit several venues at once without waiting for each venue's order-protection checks. Post-only guarantees you are the maker. Midpoint pegs buy price improvement at the risk of being picked off when the NBBO goes stale.
  • The close is a call auction. NYSE stops new MOC/LOC orders at 3:50 p.m. and Nasdaq at 3:55 p.m. Imbalance messages then invite offsetting liquidity until the 4:00 p.m. uncross.
  • The closing auction grew from about 3% of US dollar volume in 2010 to a record 9.44% of notional in Q2 2024, and about 20% on index-rebalance and expiry days.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Intuition: an order type is a contract
docs.text: Every order answers four questions: at what price (limit, market, pegged), for how long (day, IOC, on-close), may it take liquidity, and is it displayed? Exchanges list dozens of variants; most quant flow uses the few below.

docs.title: The order types that matter
docs.text:
Order type What it does Who uses it, and why Limit Trades at the limit or better; the rest rests in the book Market makers' quotes; passive child orders Market Takes whatever is there, within price collars Mostly retail; professionals use marketable limits IOC (immediate-or-cancel) Fills what is available now, cancels the rest Router probes of dark pools; taking strategies ISO (intermarket sweep) Sender certifies it is also taking out better-priced protected quotes elsewhere, so the venue may fill at once without checking away markets Routers sweeping several venues in the same microseconds; latency-sensitive takers Post-only Rejected or repriced if it would take liquidity Market makers guaranteeing the maker rebate and avoiding the taker fee Midpoint peg Non-displayed, priced at the NBBO midpoint Dark pools and exchanges; both sides save half the spread Discretionary Shown at one price, willing to trade up to a hidden worse price Institutions hiding urgency; IEX's discretionary peg also avoids stale quotes [Reported] MOC / LOC Execute only in the closing auction; LOC only at its limit or better Index funds, ETF flows, VWAP-to-close and rebalance trades MOO / LOO Same, for the opening auction Overnight-news trades, opening rebalances Imbalance-only (Nasdaq IO) and closing offset (NYSE CO) Execute only in the auction and only against the published imbalance Liquidity providers at the close

The ISO exists because of the trade-through rule (Rule 611 of Regulation NMS). On June 11, 2026 the SEC proposed rescinding that rule and the locked/crossed-market ban. Comments closed August 17, 2026, and the proposal was still pending at last check [Verified]. If it is adopted, routers' reliance on ISOs would change. Midpoint pegs are priced off someone's view of the NBBO. If that view lags, a faster trader can trade against the peg at a stale midpoint (see NBBO and market data).

docs.title: How a closing auction works
docs.text:
During the day, MOC and LOC orders build a separate closing book. At the cutoff, new entry stops, except for orders that offset the imbalance. The exchange then publishes imbalance messages: paired shares, imbalance size and side, and indicative clearing prices. Traders who can absorb the imbalance send offsetting interest. At 4:00 p.m. the auction uncrosses at one price. That price maximizes matched volume, with tie-breaks on residual imbalance and distance from a reference price, within collars [Reported]. On the NYSE a designated market maker (DMM) runs the process. The print is the official close used for NAVs and index tracking.

flowchart LR
    A1["MOC and LOC orders<br/>from index funds, ETFs, algos"] --> B1["Closing book builds<br/>through the day"]
    B1 --> C1["Entry cutoff<br/>NYSE 3:50 pm, Nasdaq 3:55 pm"]
    C1 --> D1["Imbalance messages<br/>paired shares, side, indicative price"]
    D1 --> E1["Offsetting interest arrives<br/>IO, CO, D orders, LOC"]
    E1 -.->|"updates"| D1
    E1 --> F1["4:00 pm uncross<br/>one price, maximum matched volume"]
    F1 --> G1["Official close<br/>NAV and index benchmark"]

Key times (Eastern), as of 2026-11:

Step NYSE Nasdaq Opening imbalance messages From 8:00 a.m., about every second [Verified] 9:25–9:30 a.m. [Verified] Opening order cutoff MOO/LOO cancels rejected from 9:29 a.m. [Verified] — MOC entry cutoff 3:50 p.m.; afterwards only offsetting MOC/LOC and CO [Verified] MOC before 3:55 p.m. [Verified] Closing imbalance messages From 3:50 p.m. [Verified]; floor-broker D orders included from 3:50 since August 2024 [Verified] From 3:55 p.m. (moved from 3:50 in 2018) [Verified], updated about every second [Reported] Late cutoffs No MOC/LOC cancels after 3:58 p.m. D orders accepted until 3:59:50 [Verified]; a 2026 change rejects D-order cancels from one minute before the close [Reported] TODO(verify): effective date LOC entry until 3:58 p.m. [Verified] Uncross 4:00 p.m. 4:00 p.m.

docs.title: Worked example: an imbalance moves the close
docs.text:
Illustrative numbers. XYZ last traded at $50.00. At the cutoff the closing book has 1.2M shares of MOC buys and 0.9M of MOC sells, a 300,000-share buy imbalance. Sell-side limit interest (LOC, IO and continuous-book orders) is 100,000 at $50.02, 150,000 at $50.05 and 200,000 at $50.10.

Candidate price Buy volume Sell volume Matched 50.00 1.20M 0.90M 0.90M 50.02 1.20M 1.00M 1.00M 50.05 1.20M 1.15M 1.15M 50.10 1.20M 1.35M 1.20M

The close prints at $50.10, 20 bps above the last trade: MOC buyers pay about $120,000 more than at $50.00, and sellers who offered at $50.02 get 8 cents better than their limit. That price concession is what auction liquidity providers compete for. In reality the published imbalance would attract more sellers before 4:00 p.m. and shrink the move.

docs.title: How big the close is
docs.text:
Measures differ (share vs dollar volume, NYSE-listed vs all stocks), but the trend is clear:

Period Closing auction share Measure and source 2010 about 3.1% Daily dollar volume; academic estimate [Reported] 2011 → 2017 3.6% → 5.5% Average daily volume; Greenwich Associates [Reported] 2018 about 7.5% Daily dollar volume; academic estimate [Reported] Q2 2024 9.44% (record), $55.5B/day Notional, all US equities; NYSE Research [Reported] 2024 typical day about 9%; about 20% on rebalance and expiry days Notional; BMLL [Reported] 2025, monthly 5.2%–9.7% (December 9.74%) Share volume; Rosenblatt [Reported] December 2025 about 15% (Europe about 35%) Instinet data via SSGA; broader definition, quarter-end month [Reported] 
timeline
    title US closing auction share of volume, different measures
    2010 : About 3 percent of dollar volume
    2017 : About 5.5 percent of ADV
    2018 : About 7.5 percent of dollar volume
    2024 : Record 9.44 percent of notional in Q2
    2025 : 5 to 10 percent of share volume by month

The driver is passive investing: index funds and ETFs are benchmarked to closing prices, and studies link closing volume to ETF and passive ownership rather than active ownership [Reported]. Share-volume measures run lower because cheap, retail-heavy stocks inflate daytime share counts.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• The close is a strategy venue. Auctions and closing liquidity is about supplying the imbalance. Flow-driven strategies and ETF and index arbitrage trade around rebalance prints.
  • Execution algos are built from these order types. Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos decide what to send to the close. VWAP, TWAP and POV must forecast the close's slice of the volume curve. Smart order routing chooses between IOC, ISO and midpoint pegs.
  • Order types are where fees and adverse selection meet. Post-only rebate capture is the base of equity market making and fee- and microstructure-driven strategies. Stale midpoint pegs are prey for latency arbitrage. Queue position and order placement treats the choice of order type as part of the placement decision.

docs.title: Recent changes (as of 2026-11)
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Live: price-tiered round lots (Nov 3, 2025), best odd-lot orders on the SIP (late April 2026), amended Rule 605 execution-quality reports (Aug 1, 2026) and T+1 settlement (May 28, 2024).
  • Deferred: the half-penny tick and the 0.10¢ access-fee cap are pushed to Nov 1, 2027 and back under review. Form SHO and securities-lending reporting are pushed to 2028–2029.
  • Coming: 23-hour weekday stock trading on Nasdaq, NYSE Arca and the SIPs, targeted for Dec 6, 2026. A proposal to repeal the trade-through rule (June 2026) is pending.
  • Growing: 0DTE options set a record 66.2% of SPX volume in July 2026.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

This page keeps only changes that alter a strategy's P&L, data or risk. Each item was checked in November 2026 against regulators' releases, exchange notices or law-firm and trade-press summaries. The tag on each row says which. Dates and statuses move, so re-check before relying on any row.

docs.title: What each change means
docs.text:
The pricing grid: ticks, fees and lots. The round-lot change is live and it matters. In stocks priced above $250, the NBBO is now set by 40-, 10- or 1-share orders, so the protected quote is tighter and thinner. Signals built on NBBO size or on the spread shifted level on Nov 3, 2025, so treat that date as a break in any history. Half-penny ticks and the lower fee cap would rewrite market-maker unit economics (worked example in fees, rebates and ticks). Compliance moved from Nov 2025 to Nov 2026 by an Oct 31, 2025 order, then to Nov 1, 2027 by a June 2026 order. The Chairman has also asked staff to review both rules [Reported]. Treat the 2027 date as provisional.

Market data and disclosure. Since late April 2026, SIP subscribers can see the best odd-lot order, which narrows the information gap between SIP and direct feeds a little. The full odd-lot depth between that order and the NBBO waits until May 2028 [Verified]. The amended Rule 605 applies from Aug 1, 2026. It brings in large brokers and single-dealer platforms, adds millisecond time-to-execution, and measures price improvement against the best displayed price including odd lots [Verified]. That gives better public data for judging wholesaler execution quality and for TCA.

Routing rules. On Jun 11, 2026 the SEC proposed rescinding Rule 611 (trade-through) and Rule 610(e) (locked and crossed markets) [Verified]. One sell-side analyst expects a final rule in early 2027 [Reported]. If adopted, routers would no longer be forced to honor the best protected quote at every venue, and the case for fee-, fill- and markout-weighted routing would get stronger. The Gensler-era retail auction (Order Competition Rule) and the Reg Best Execution proposal were withdrawn on Jun 12, 2025 [Reported], so the wholesaler model described in venues and retail flow stands.

Trading hours. The SEC approved Nasdaq's 23-hour weekday schedule on Apr 10, 2026. Other exchanges followed, and the SIP plans approved matching hours [Reported]. The target is Dec 6, 2026. The schedule runs from 9 p.m. ET Sunday to 8 p.m. ET Friday, with a one-hour pause each weekday evening, and opens with static 20% overnight price bands [Reported]. 24X National Exchange has traded 4 a.m.–8 p.m. ET since October 2025 [Reported]. An Aug 7, 2026 SEC order lets 24X run overnight without SIP coverage from Jan 24, 2027, but only if the SIPs miss their date [Verified]. For strategies, overnight cash trading would weaken futures' monopoly on overnight price discovery. It would create new ETF market-making and event-driven windows, and risk systems would have to treat the "close" differently. Expect thin liquidity early on.

Options. 0DTE share keeps rising: a 66.2% record in July 2026 [Verified], and about 3.4M contracts a day in Q3 2026 [Reported]. Intraday hedging flow and the volatility debate are covered in ETF, futures and options linkages.

Settlement and shorting. T+1 is settled practice. After the Fifth Circuit's August 2025 remand, the SEC pushed the short-sale and securities-lending transparency rules to 2028–2029 [Reported]. Short-side crowding data therefore still comes from vendors and FINRA short interest (see shorting, financing and settlement).

Watch list. The SEC's Sep 17, 2026 innovation exemption allows capped on-chain trading of tokenized US-listed stocks for five years [Reported]. On Nov 3, 2026, the CFTC Chairman said single-stock perpetual futures may trade on venues also registered with the SEC [Reported]. Neither affects mainstream strategies yet. Both could become new hedging or arbitrage legs. On the CAT, the 2023 funding model was vacated by the Eleventh Circuit in 2025, a revised funding order followed in March 2026, and an April 2026 concept release opened a wider review [Reported].

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• The pricing grid. Equity market making and fee- and microstructure-driven strategies need scenario P&L for the 2027 tick and fee change, and they must re-baseline features at the Nov 2025 round-lot break. Their tools are quoting and inventory control and queue position.
  • Market data. Order-book and trade-flow signals and fair value and microprice change their inputs with odd-lot data. Point-in-time data must record the rule-change dates.
  • Routing. Smart order routing, latency arbitrage and retail flow internalization depend on how Rule 611 and Rule 605 turn out.
  • Trading hours. 23-hour trading affects ETF market making, lead-lag arbitrage, earnings and event-driven trading and algorithmic risk controls.
  • Options. 0DTE growth reshapes options market making and the volatility risk premium, and it changes the inputs to hedging algorithms.

docs.title: Shorting, financing and settlement
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A short sale needs three things. The broker needs a locate before the order (Reg SHO Rule 203). Someone has to lend the shares, at a floating fee. And you carry recall risk for as long as the position is open.
  • Borrow cost is skewed. Most large caps are general collateral at a fraction of a percent a year. A thin tail of hard-to-borrow names costs 5% to 50% or more, and that tail is often where the "alpha" in short signals sits.
  • Rule 201 forces passive shorting after a 10% drop. Rule 204 forces the close-out of failed deliveries. T+1 settlement (since May 28, 2024) shortens every step.
  • Prime-broker financing spreads plus borrow fees can take a quarter or more of a long-short book's gross alpha.
  • The new short-position (Form SHO) and securities-lending (Rule 10c-1a) transparency rules are deferred to 2028–2029 (as of 2026-11).

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: The life of a short
docs.text:
To a portfolio manager a short is one order. To the plumbing it is a chain of obligations that runs from the trade until the shares are returned.

sequenceDiagram
    participant PM as Portfolio manager
    participant PB as Prime broker
    participant LND as Lender (agent lender or fund)
    participant MKT as Exchange and clearing
    PM->>PB: Locate request (or check easy-to-borrow list)
    PB-->>PM: Locate granted, indicative fee
    PM->>MKT: Sell short on trade date T
    PB->>LND: Borrow shares, post cash collateral
    PB->>MKT: Deliver shares at settlement (T+1)
    loop Every day the short is open
        LND-->>PB: Fee reprices with supply and demand
    end
    LND->>PB: Recall (lender sells or votes)
    PB-->>PM: Re-borrow elsewhere, or buy in

docs.title: Locates and borrow fees
docs.text:
The locate. Under Rule 203(b)(1), a broker-dealer may not accept or effect a short sale unless it has borrowed the shares, has arranged to borrow them, or has reasonable grounds to believe they can be borrowed for delivery when due. The locate has to be documented. Bona fide market makers are exempt [Verified]. That exemption is what lets an equity market maker sell to a buyer before it owns the stock. In practice, prime brokers publish a daily easy-to-borrow list, and every other name needs an explicit locate against limited supply [Lore].

The fee. Shares come from lenders such as index funds, pensions and insurers, usually through agent lenders. The borrower posts cash collateral, conventionally about 102% of the loan's value [Lore]. The lender pays interest back on that cash, called the rebate rate: the benchmark rate minus the borrow fee. When a name is scarce, the rebate goes negative, which means the borrower pays on top of giving up interest.

Bucket Typical fee (annualized) Where you find it General collateral (GC) about 0.25–0.50% [Lore] most large and mid caps Warm about 0.5–5% [Lore] small caps, crowded shorts Hard-to-borrow / special 5–50%+, occasionally triple digits [Lore] squeezes, recent IPOs, heavily shorted names

The academic evidence agrees on the shape. In D'Avolio's 2000–2001 data, about nine in ten stocks lent at under 1% a year, and a small set of "specials" carried most of the cost [Reported].

The fee is a floating rate on an open-ended loan. Lenders can recall at any time. The fee reprices daily, so a name that costs 1% today can cost 30% in a squeeze. Engelberg, Reed and Ringgenberg (2018) show that this short-selling risk deters arbitrage and goes with more mispricing [Reported]. Drechsler and Drechsler (2014) find that much of the return to well-known anomalies is concentrated in high-fee stocks [Reported]. In other words, the "alpha" on many short signals is partly a fee you would have to pay to collect it.

docs.title: Rule 201, Rule 204 and T+1
docs.text:
• Rule 201 (short-sale circuit breaker). When a stock falls 10% or more from the prior day's close, short sales for the rest of that day and all of the next day may only be priced above the current national best bid. A few narrow exemptions are marked "short exempt" [Verified]. In effect, a short seller can no longer hit the bid. The short leg of a mean-reversion trade after a crash has to rest passively, and it may not fill.
  • Rule 204 (close-out). A fail to deliver from a short sale must be closed out by the market open on the day after settlement, which is T+2 under T+1. Fails from long sales and from bona fide market making get until the third settlement day after settlement, T+4 [Verified]. A broker that misses the deadline is barred from further shorts in that stock until it pre-borrows. Traders call this the "penalty box".
  • T+1 settlement. US equities moved from T+2 to T+1 on May 28, 2024 [Verified]. Trades must also be affirmed on trade date. For short sellers this means less time to source a borrow, faster buy-ins after a recall, and a tighter calendar around corporate actions and ETF creations.

docs.title: Financing through a prime broker
docs.text:
A prime broker finances longs and lends shorts:

  • Long side. The debit balance is charged at a benchmark rate (SOFR, OBFR or Fed funds) plus a spread, about 30–75 bp for a large fund [Lore].
  • Short side. Short proceeds earn the benchmark minus a spread. That spread is effectively the GC fee. HTB fees come on top.
  • Leverage. Reg T sets a 50% initial margin and FINRA Rule 4210 a 25% long maintenance margin [Verified]. Hedge funds mostly use risk-based house or portfolio margin instead. Under it, equity market-neutral books typically run about 4–8x gross leverage [Lore].
  • Swaps. Total return swaps carry the same economics but sit on the dealer's balance sheet, so pricing moves with the dealer's capital costs.

docs.title: Worked example: borrow and financing drag
docs.text:
Take an illustrative dollar-neutral book with $250M of capital, $500M long and $500M short (4x gross). In a dollar-neutral book the benchmark interest roughly nets out. What is left are the spreads and fees.

Cost line Calculation Annual cost Long financing spread 0.40% × $500M $2.00M GC borrow on 90% of shorts 0.30% × $450M $1.35M HTB borrow on 10% of shorts 8% average × $50M $4.00M Total drag $7.35M = 2.9% of capital

If the gross alpha is 10% on capital ($25M), carrying the book eats about 29% of it. The 10% of shorts that are hard to borrow cost more than the whole GC book and the long financing combined. That is why production systems treat borrow cost as a per-name negative expected return, cap or exclude HTB names, and build recall risk into sizing. A backtest that ignores this overstates short-side returns exactly where the signal looks strongest.

flowchart LR
    G["Gross alpha<br/>$25.0M"] --> B1["minus HTB borrow<br/>$4.0M"]
    B1 --> B2["minus long financing spread<br/>$2.0M"]
    B2 --> B3["minus GC borrow<br/>$1.35M"]
    B3 --> N["Net before trading costs<br/>$17.65M"]

docs.title: Disclosure rules in limbo (as of 2026-11)
docs.text:
• Rule 13f-2 / Form SHO. Institutional managers above set thresholds ($10M, or a 2.5% monthly average of shares outstanding, for reporting issuers) would report gross short positions monthly [Reported]. The SEC would publish aggregates.
  • Rule 10c-1a. Lenders would report loan terms, including fees, to FINRA for publication.
  • Status. In August 2025 the Fifth Circuit remanded both rules to the SEC without vacating them. On Dec 3, 2025, the SEC deferred compliance to Jan 2, 2028 for Form SHO (first filings due Feb 14, 2028), and to Sep 28, 2028 for 10c-1a reporting, with public dissemination from Mar 29, 2029 [Reported].

Until then, borrow data comes from commercial securities-finance vendors and FINRA's twice-monthly short-interest reports.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Short-heavy books. Factor-residual mean reversion, pairs trading, cross-sectional alpha and value, quality and low vol all carry the drag above. Their short legs are where borrow constraints bind.
  • Rule 201 and recalls. These bite short-term reversal and earnings and event-driven trades when they matter most.
  • Market makers. ETF and index arbitrage and options market making rely on the market-maker locate exception and price borrow into parity.
  • Algorithms.
    • Mean-variance optimization and transaction cost and impact models take borrow as a cost or constraint.
    • Position sizing and risk budgeting handles recall risk.
    • Backtest pitfalls covers the cost of ignoring borrow.
    • Live monitoring and P&L attribution reports financing as its own P&L line.

docs.title: The limit order book
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A limit order book (LOB) is the list of resting buy and sell limit orders on one venue, sorted by price and, within each price, by arrival time. Marketable orders consume it from the best price outward.
  • Price-time priority makes your place in the queue an asset. An early order gets more fills, and its fills are less adversely selected, than an identical order at the back.
  • Hidden and iceberg orders trade visibility for priority: they hide size but queue behind displayed orders at the same price.
  • What execution algos and market makers care about is depth (how much trades near the touch) and resilience (how fast the book refills after a sweep), not just the spread.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Intuition: a queue at every price
docs.text:
Picture a row of ticket windows, one per price, with buyers (or sellers) lined up at each in arrival order. A seller who wants to trade now goes to the highest bid window and serves the line from the front. The limit order book is exactly this, kept by each exchange's matching engine.

Three events change the book:

  • Add: a non-marketable limit order joins the back of the queue at its price.
  • Cancel: a resting order leaves. Most US equity orders are cancelled, not filled.
  • Execute: a marketable order matches against the front of the best opposite queue.

On US exchanges the minimum quoting increment (tick size) is $0.01 for stocks priced at $1 or more. The SEC's 2024 amendments add a $0.005 tick for stocks whose spread is pinned at one tick, but compliance has been pushed to the first business day of November 2027 [Verified]. See fees, rebates and ticks.

flowchart TD
    N1["Incoming order"] --> Q1{"Marketable?<br/>buy limit at or above best ask"}
    Q1 -->|"no"| R1["Rest in book at its price,<br/>behind earlier orders"]
    Q1 -->|"yes"| M1["Match the best opposite level,<br/>oldest order first"]
    M1 --> Q2{"Quantity left?"}
    Q2 -->|"no"| F1["Fully filled"]
    Q2 -->|"yes"| Q3{"Next level still<br/>within the limit?"}
    Q3 -->|"yes"| M1
    Q3 -->|"no"| Q4{"Time in force"}
    Q4 -->|"IOC"| C1["Cancel the remainder"]
    Q4 -->|"Day or GTC"| R1

docs.title: Price-time priority
docs.text:
Matching follows price-time priority: better price first, then earlier arrival (FIFO) within a price. Most US equity venues use strict FIFO; some options markets allocate pro rata by size instead [Lore]. Priority is fragile: reducing size usually keeps your place, while changing price or increasing size sends you to the back with a new timestamp.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Resting: post limit order
    Resting --> Resting: size reduced, keeps priority
    Resting --> Requeued: price change or size increase
    Requeued --> Resting: new timestamp at back of queue
    Resting --> PartFilled: partial execution
    PartFilled --> Filled: remainder executes
    Resting --> Filled: full execution
    Resting --> Cancelled: cancel
    PartFilled --> Cancelled: cancel remainder
    Filled --> [*]
    Cancelled --> [*]

docs.title: Worked example: a market order walks the book
docs.text:
An illustrative book for stock XYZ on one exchange (sizes in shares, order IDs in brackets):

Bid size Bid Ask Ask size 600 [G 600] 100.00 100.01 400 [E 100, F 300] 800 99.99 100.02 500 [C 200, D 300] 1,500 99.98 100.03 300 [A 100, B 200]

The mid is 100.005 and the spread is one tick. A market buy for 1,000 shares arrives:

  • 400 at 100.01 (E first, then F, by time)
  • 500 at 100.02 (C, then D)
  • 100 at 100.03 (A; B is untouched)

Average price = (400 × 100.01 + 500 × 100.02 + 100 × 100.03) / 1,000 = 100.017. That is 1.2 cents, or about 1.2 bps, above the pre-trade mid: $12 of cost on a $100k order. The book after the trade shows 100.00 bid and 100.03 ask, a 3-cent spread. How fast market makers re-quote 100.01 and 100.02 is the book's resilience; in liquid names it is often milliseconds [Lore]. In practice a router would sweep several venues at once with ISOs rather than walk one book (see order types and auctions). Lab 01 implements a price-time matching engine you can replay this on.

docs.title: Queue value: why being early is worth money
docs.text:
Take a large-tick stock where the spread is almost always one cent and 10,000 shares sit on the best bid. Compare joining that bid as the first 500 shares in line with joining as the last 500.

  1. Fill probability. The front gets filled by ordinary small sell orders. The back is filled only if enough selling arrives to chew through 9,500 shares ahead of it.
  2. Adverse selection. When the back does get filled, it is usually because a large or informed seller is sweeping the level, and the price then ticks down. A back-of-queue fill is a signal that you just bought before a drop.

Illustrative numbers, per share, for a resting bid that gets filled. The markout is the mid's move against you shortly after the fill.

Front of queue Back of queue Half-spread earned vs mid +0.50¢ +0.50¢ Maker rebate +0.20¢ +0.20¢ Markout (adverse selection) −0.20¢ −0.90¢ Net if filled +0.50¢ −0.20¢ Fill probability over the next minute 90% 30% Expected value per share posted +0.45¢ −0.06¢

The front is worth about half a cent a share more than the back, roughly the half-spread, a common rule of thumb for large-tick names [Lore]. Most of the gap is adverse selection, not fill rate. That is why HFT market makers race to the front when a new price level opens, and why the queue-position card models the two together. Academic queue models include Cont, Stoikov and Talreja (2010) and Huang, Lehalle and Rosenbaum's queue-reactive model (2015).

docs.title: Hidden and iceberg orders
docs.text:
• Non-displayed (hidden) orders rest in the book but are not shown on market data. On most venues they rank behind displayed orders at the same price, so hiding costs priority. Midpoint pegs are usually non-displayed.
  • Iceberg (reserve) orders show a small tip, for example 100 shares, and refill from a hidden reserve. Each refill normally gets a new timestamp, so the visible part keeps going to the back of the line.
  • Detection. Prints larger than the visible size, or a level that keeps refilling after being hit, reveal hidden interest.

docs.title: Depth and resilience
docs.text:
Depth is how much you can trade within k ticks of the mid. It differs by stock type:

  • Large-tick stocks (low price, high volume) have a spread stuck at one tick and long queues. Cost is mostly waiting time and queue position.
  • Small-tick stocks (high price) have spreads of many ticks and thin levels. Cost is mostly walking the book.

Displayed depth understates true liquidity (hidden, off-exchange and reactive interest is missing) and overstates it (quotes vanish when price starts to move). Resilience is the speed at which spread and depth recover after a sweep. Part of a trade's price impact is transient (the book refills) and part is permanent (information). That split is the core of transaction cost and impact models. Kyle (1985) formalized depth as the price move per unit of order flow, Kyle's lambda.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Market making is queue management. Equity market making and fee- and microstructure-driven strategies earn the spread and rebate only from positions near the front. See queue position and order placement, quoting and inventory control and adverse selection and markouts.
  • The book is a signal. Queue sizes at the touch feed the microprice and order-flow imbalance. Short-horizon forecasts in ML-driven short-horizon alpha start from these features.
  • Walking the book is a cost. The worked example is the micro version of what impact models estimate and what VWAP, TWAP and POV and smart order routing try to avoid.
  • Stale queues get picked off. Latency arbitrage races to hit resting orders before they are cancelled.

docs.title: Venues and retail flow
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • US stocks trade on 18 exchanges (as of October 2026), 33 NMS-stock ATSs and over 200 other off-exchange dealers. In 2025 off-exchange volume was 50.6% of the total, the first annual majority, and about four-fifths of it went through principal dealers such as wholesalers.
  • Wholesalers pay retail brokers for marketable orders (PFOF) because retail flow is "less toxic": it rarely predicts the next price move. They can give price improvement and still earn a spread.
  • Flow toxicity is measured by markouts: how far the price moves against the liquidity provider after the fill.
  • Of the SEC's four December 2022 proposals, two were adopted (Rule 605 disclosure; ticks, access fees and round lots) and two were withdrawn in June 2025 (the Order Competition Rule and Regulation Best Execution).

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Wholesalers and payment for order flow
docs.text:
When the SEC proposed its Order Competition Rule in December 2022, it found that brokers sent more than 90% of individual investors' marketable orders to six wholesalers [Verified]. Academic work using 2019–2022 data finds that two of them, Citadel Securities and Virtu, handled over 70% of US retail flow [Reported]. Wholesalers fill those orders as principal at or better than the NBBO, usually with price improvement, and pay the broker PFOF. Robinhood's 2025 Rule 606 reports show payments from tens of cents to about a dollar per 100 shares, depending on wholesaler, order type and stock group [Reported]. Citadel Securities paid about $341M for US retail equity and options flow in Q2 2025 alone [Reported].

A wholesaler's per-share income statement for a 100-share retail buy (illustrative: $50 stock, NBBO $49.99 × $50.01):

Line ¢ per share Sell at $50.006 (0.4¢ price improvement); spread captured vs mid $50.00 +0.60 Adverse selection: mid drifts 0.10¢ up over the next minute −0.10 PFOF to the broker −0.15 Hedging, exchange fees, clearing, technology −0.10 Net +0.25

Run the same fill against an informed taker whose one-minute markout is 1.5¢ and the result is −1.15¢. The whole business rests on being able to tell those two counterparties apart.

docs.title: Flow toxicity: why retail is "less toxic"
docs.text:
Flow toxicity is the probability-weighted damage a counterparty does to a liquidity provider. It is the expected price move against you after you trade with them. Glosten and Milgrom (1985) showed that a dealer facing some informed traders must widen the spread to everyone. VPIN (Easley, López de Prado and O'Hara, 2012) estimates toxicity from volume imbalance. Practitioners mostly measure it directly with markouts. The realized spread is the effective spread minus the subsequent price move.

Retail marketable orders are small, uncorrelated across accounts and rarely timed on information that matters over the next seconds to minutes, so their markouts are small. The key difference is segmentation. A wholesaler knows which broker sent the order, so it knows the flow is retail. An exchange sees anonymous orders and must price for the average counterparty. The two sides of the debate:

  • For the current model: retail gets better-than-NBBO fills and zero commissions, paid for by the low cost of serving uninformed flow.
  • Against: the SEC estimated a $1.5B-a-year "competitive shortfall" versus order-by-order auctions [Verified]. Critics also argue that taking benign flow off exchanges leaves lit quotes facing more toxic flow, so lit spreads are wider for everyone.

The evidence is mixed. This KB takes no side.

    x-axis Low urgency --> High urgency
    y-axis Low information --> High information

    quadrant-2 Patient informed

    quadrant-4 Urgent but uninformed
