docs.title: Disclosure: Rules 605 and 606
docs.text:
• Rule 605 requires monthly execution-quality statistics: effective spreads, price improvement and speed. The March 6, 2024 amendments extend it to brokers with 100,000 or more customer accounts, add a summary report, and add realized spreads at several horizons from 50 ms to 5 minutes [Reported]. Compliance moved from December 14, 2025 to August 1, 2026 [Verified]. Short-horizon realized spreads are, in effect, standardized public markouts.
  • Rule 606 requires quarterly broker routing reports: where orders went and the PFOF received per 100 shares.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Retail flow is a strategy. Retail flow internalization is the wholesaler business above. Its risk model is adverse selection and markouts, and its pricing engine is fair value and microprice.
  • Toxicity sets the quote. Equity market making and quoting and inventory control widen or skew quotes on toxicity estimates. Latency arbitrage is the most toxic flow there is.
  • Venue choice is an algorithm. Smart order routing ranks venues by fill rate and post-fill markout. Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos handle the dark pools. Transaction cost analysis audits the result.

docs.title: Strategies: the map
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • This module has 30 strategy dossiers in seven families (A–G), plus five cross-cutting pages (H). Every dossier follows one template, so any two compare directly.
  • Every strategy sits at a point on two axes: holding horizon (microseconds to months) and edge source (speed · liquidity provision · structural/regulatory · informational · behavioral · risk premium).
  • Short horizons are dominated by liquidity provision, speed and structure; long horizons by risk premia and behavioral effects. Informational edges sit in the middle.
  • Most "stat arb" is liquidity provision on a slower clock: you are paid for absorbing other people's price pressure.
  • Read every dossier's header table first. If you only remember one row, make it "Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it."

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Three lessons. First, horizon and edge are correlated, not identical: liquidity provision runs from microseconds (quoting) to weeks (pairs), because absorbing price pressure is paid at every horizon (Grossman and Miller; Nagel) [Verified]. Second, capacity rises with horizon while Sharpe falls; the comparison matrix puts numbers on it. Third, the middle is the most crowded: days-to-weeks informational and behavioral signals are where most quant funds and pods compete, and where published signals decay fastest (evaluation).

docs.title: How to read a dossier
docs.text:
Every dossier opens with this header table:

Field What it tells you How to read it Family Which of the seven groups (A–G) Families share data, infrastructure and failure modes Edge source Primary edge first, then secondary The six-way taxonomy is defined in How quants evaluate a strategy Holding period Typical life of a position Sets infrastructure, turnover and how fast you learn the strategy is broken Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it The economic victim or customer If nobody identifiable pays, assume the backtest is lying Universe & instruments What gets traded and hedged Wider universes add breadth; illiquid names add cost Data required Inputs, from direct feeds to filings to alt data Drives cost and point-in-time risk Core algorithms used The 2–6 central module 03 cards Feeds the strategy × algorithm matrix Infra intensity Latency sensitivity and compute Says whether a microsecond, or a GPU cluster, matters Capacity (rough $ range) Money one firm can run before costs eat the edge Always tagged, with reasoning; treat as an order of magnitude Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Risk-adjusted return before and after costs Look for period, source type and decay; an academic backtest is an upper bound Turnover How often the book trades Turnover × cost per dollar traded = cost drag Main risks / failure modes How it loses money Mechanisms plus dated episodes Crowding risk How many others hold the same positions Crowded trades fail together, fast Firm types that run it Types from the big picture Named firms only when sourced Lab A runnable synthetic-data lab, if any Toy markets; each lab lists what it misses

Confidence tags. [Verified] means a primary source (filing, regulator, paper, exchange document). [Reported] means credible press, survey or practitioner book. [Estimate] means our derivation, with the reasoning shown. [Lore] means widely repeated but unverified. Every Sharpe ratio, capacity or return figure states gross or net, the period, the source type (academic backtest, fund disclosure, practitioner estimate) and known post-publication decay.

The body always runs: intuition → economic rationale → the trade → worked example → algorithms and pseudocode → implementation → P&L decomposition → evidence → capacity and decay → failures → textbook vs practice → variants → diagram → practitioner talk → myths → questions to ask (🔒 = proprietary territory) → collapsible math.

docs.title: How quants evaluate a strategy
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Every strategy is a claim that someone will keep paying you. The first test is naming that payer and one of six edge sources: risk premium, behavioral, structural/regulatory, informational, liquidity provision, speed.
  • Judge the net Sharpe, not the gross. Breakeven cost is gross alpha ÷ turnover; at high turnover, a haircut to gross alpha becomes a much larger haircut to net alpha.
  • A new strategy improves a book only if its Sharpe exceeds ρ × the book's Sharpe. A mediocre, uncorrelated strategy often beats a brilliant clone.
  • Backtests shrink live: published anomalies lost 26% out-of-sample and 58% after publication in one large study [Verified]. Plan on a haircut.
  • Funding is staged (shadow, small capital, ramp) with kill criteria written down before the first trade. Months of live P&L cannot prove alpha; they can prove the implementation.

Level: Core · Read time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11

A strategy pitch is a business plan: a revenue source (the edge), a customer (the counterparty), a cost base, a market size (capacity) and a risk of sudden death. A PM or CIO interrogates it like an acquisition: is the revenue real, will it last, what does it cost, and what does it do to the rest of the portfolio?

docs.title: The six edge sources
docs.text:
Each edge source has its own reason to persist and its own way to die.

Edge source You are paid for Why it persists How it dies Examples Risk premium Holding a risk others want to shed (crashes, distress, illiquidity) The risk is real: it periodically hurts, so the premium is a fair price Rarely dies; compresses when capital floods in Factors, VRP, carry Behavioral Other investors' systematic errors: under-reaction, extrapolation, anchoring Biases are human; arbitrage is limited by risk and career risk Publication and crowding arbitrage it down Momentum, earnings drift, revisions Structural / regulatory Someone forced by a rule or mandate to trade at a bad price Lasts as long as the rule or the mandate Rule changes, or competitors bid the edge to zero Flow-driven, auctions, fee-driven Informational Knowing or processing something sooner or better Data is scarce or hard to process The data commoditizes: vendors sell it to everyone Alt data, NLP Liquidity provision Immediacy for impatient traders, plus bearing inventory risk and adverse selection Demand for immediacy never goes away Margins are competed down; only scale survives Market making, reversal Speed Reacting first to public information Latency differences always exist somewhere Winner-take-most arms race; everyone but the fastest is priced out Latency arbitrage, lead-lag

Our view [Estimate] (reasoning: the persistence column): edges where the counterparty has a lasting reason to pay (risk premia, liquidity provision, rules) are the most durable. Informational and behavioral signals at days-to-weeks horizons are the least durable, because they are the easiest to copy.

docs.title: The evaluation checklist
docs.text: # Question Red flag 1 Economic rationale: why should this make money? "The model found it" 2 Counterparty: who pays, and why do they accept it? No identifiable payer 3 Sharpe or IR, gross and net, with significance Only gross shown; short sample; hundreds of variants tried 4 Capacity: dollars before costs eat the edge Capacity quoted without an impact model 5 Turnover and cost sensitivity Breakeven cost within 2× of the modeled cost 6 Correlation to the existing book Fails the ρ × Sharpe hurdle 7 Tail risk Smooth returns from selling insurance 8 Decay No out-of-sample or post-publication period 9 Crowding Same positions as published factors or peers 10 Data and infrastructure cost Fixed costs larger than expected net alpha at realistic size

docs.title: Sharpe and IR: gross vs net, and why short horizons win
docs.text:
The Sharpe ratio is excess return over volatility; the information ratio applies it to active return. Only the net figure pays anyone.

Short-horizon strategies post higher Sharpe ratios because they make many small, nearly independent bets; annualized Sharpe scales with the square root of independent bets per year. A daily Sharpe of 0.2 annualizes to 0.2 × √252 ≈ 3.2. Virtu's 2014 IPO filing showed one losing day in 1,238 [Reported]. If daily P&L were normal, that would imply a daily Sharpe near 3.2 and an annualized figure around 50 [Estimate] (illustrative; P&L has fat tails). The price of that Sharpe is capacity: such books cannot absorb billions.

Confidence grows slowly: the t-statistic is roughly Sharpe × √years, so a true Sharpe of 0.75 needs about seven years to reach t = 2. Lo (2002) shows serial correlation can distort annualized Sharpe ratios [Verified]. Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue a new factor needs t > 3, not 2, given how many have been tried [Verified]. The deflated Sharpe ratio of Bailey and López de Prado corrects for the number of trials and for non-normality [Verified] (see overfitting and multiple testing).

docs.title: Turnover, costs and breakeven
docs.text:
Let gross alpha be \(\alpha\) (per year, as a fraction of gross market value), turnover \(T\) (dollars traded per year ÷ GMV, both sides counted) and all-in cost \(c\) per dollar traded (spread, fees, market impact). Then:

\[ \alpha_{net} = \alpha - T\,c, \qquad c^{*} = \frac{\alpha}{T} \]

The sensitivity of net alpha to cost is \(-T\): every extra basis point of cost subtracts \(T\) basis points of return.

Illustrative strategy Gross α Turnover T Breakeven c* Modeled cost Net α +1 bp of cost costs you Monthly factor book 3% 6× 50 bp 10 bp 2.4% 0.06% a year Daily residual reversal 12% 60× 20 bp 8 bp 7.2% 0.6% a year Intraday stat arb 25% 500× 5 bp 3 bp 10% 5% a year

Novy-Marx and Velikov agree: most anomalies with under 50% monthly one-sided turnover survive costs; few higher-turnover ones do [Verified]. Cost models are covered in P5; measuring realized cost in E6.

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text: Capacity is the size at which marginal net alpha reaches zero, or net Sharpe hits the hurdle; impact rises roughly with the square root of participation. An AQR study using live execution data estimated break-even fund sizes for US long-short size, value and momentum factors of roughly $52–103B [Reported] (2012 draft; one manager's costs). For latency-sensitive strategies, capacity is better counted in P&L than in capital: the edge per trade is a fraction of a tick, and the whole global latency-arbitrage pool in equities has been estimated at about $5B a year (Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill) [Reported].

docs.title: Correlation to the book: the marginal Sharpe test
docs.text:
Adding a small allocation to a new strategy raises the book's Sharpe only if

\[ SR_{new} > \rho \cdot SR_{book} \]

where \(\rho\) is the correlation between the new strategy and the existing book (derivation below; see also Benhamou and Guez). With an existing book at Sharpe 2.0:

Candidate Standalone Sharpe ρ to book Hurdle ρ × 2.0 Book Sharpe after optimal mix A: decent, mildly correlated 0.8 0.3 0.6 2.01 B: same, uncorrelated 0.8 0.0 0.0 2.15 C: weak, negatively correlated 0.6 −0.3 −0.6 2.36 D: strong clone 1.5 0.8 1.6 2.00 (optimal weight is zero)

Candidate C, the weakest standalone, adds the most; D, the best on paper, adds nothing. Caveats: correlations jump toward one in a crisis (in August 2007 many quant equity books unwound the same positions at once, per Khandani and Lo [Verified]); and a strategy that barely moves the book's Sharpe can still be worth funding if the book is at capacity.

docs.title: Tail risk, decay, crowding and cost of doing business
docs.text:
• Tail risk. Sharpe treats upside and downside alike. Insurance-selling strategies (short volatility, carry, much liquidity provision) show smooth returns and negative skew. Ask for the worst day, week and month; Khandani and Lo's simulated market maker lost heavily in the week of August 6, 2007 [Verified]. See the failure gallery.
  • Decay. Across 97 published predictors, returns were 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower after publication (McLean and Pontiff) [Verified]. Falck, Rej and Thesmar find out-of-sample performance around half of in-sample, with publication date the main predictor of alpha decay [Verified]. Monitor live decay with L2.
  • Crowding. Warning signs: P&L correlated with published factors or peers, falling alpha per unit of turnover, violent reversals on de-risking days (crowding).
  • Data and infrastructure. Investment managers spent roughly $2.8B on alternative data in 2025, up 17% [Reported]. Fixed costs set a minimum size: a $1M-a-year dataset needs $25M of GMV at 4% net alpha to pay for itself [Estimate]. For HFT, colocation, feeds and hardware make breakeven a dollar figure, not a basis-point one.

docs.title: How a PM or CIO decides to fund a strategy
docs.text:
Funding is staged so that each dollar buys information: research review (the checklist) → shadow trading (live signals, no capital) → small capital (enough to measure real costs and fills) → ramp in steps, re-estimating impact at each size → steady state and retirement, with kill criteria set in advance.

Pods use hard drawdown limits. Widely reported Millennium practice: a PM's capital is roughly halved at a 5% drawdown and the PM is usually out near 7.5% (some accounts say 10%) [Reported]; firms do not publish these rules.

flowchart TD
    A["New strategy idea"] --> B{"Named counterparty<br/>and edge source?"}
    B -->|"no"| K["Reject"]
    B -->|"yes"| C{"Net Sharpe after costs<br/>and trial haircut clears hurdle?"}
    C -->|"no"| R["Redesign: cut turnover,<br/>widen universe, combine"]
    R --> C
    C -->|"yes"| D{"Beats rho times<br/>book Sharpe?"}
    D -->|"no"| K
    D -->|"yes"| E{"Capacity pays for<br/>data and infrastructure?"}
    E -->|"no"| K
    E -->|"yes"| F["Shadow trading"]
    F --> G["Small capital"]
    G --> H{"Costs, fills and tracking<br/>match the model?"}
    H -->|"no"| R
    H -->|"yes"| I["Ramp in steps"]
    I --> J["Monitor decay and crowding"]
    J -->|"kill criteria hit"| Z["Cut or retire"]

docs.title: Worked example (illustrative numbers)
docs.text:
A researcher proposes a 1–3 day residual-reversal strategy on ~1,000 liquid US stocks. Backtest 2014–2025 (12 years); 200 parameter variants tried. Gross alpha 12% of GMV a year at 4% volatility (gross Sharpe 3.0); turnover 60×; modeled cost 8 bp per dollar traded, so net alpha 7.2% (net Sharpe 1.8). Correlation to the existing book is 0.3; the book runs at Sharpe 2.0.

  1. Is it noise? Over 12 years the standard error of an annual Sharpe is about 1/√12 ≈ 0.29, so the best of 200 independent zero-alpha variants would show about 2.75 × 0.29 ≈ 0.8 by luck. Net 1.8 clears that bar.
  2. Haircut gross, not net. Apply a 30–50% decay haircut (the range from the studies above) to gross alpha: 6.0–8.4%. Costs stay at 4.8% (60 × 8 bp), so net becomes 1.2–3.6%, Sharpe 0.3–0.9. A 50% haircut to gross is an 83% haircut to net.
  3. Marginal test. The hurdle is 0.3 × 2.0 = 0.6. The planning range of 0.3–0.9 straddles it. Not fundable as designed.
  4. Redesign. A no-trade band and trading toward the aim cut turnover to 35× while keeping, say, 80% of gross alpha (9.6%). Costs drop to 2.8%. After the same haircut: net 2.0–3.9%, Sharpe 0.5–1.0. The midpoint (0.75) clears 0.6; the low end does not, which is why it gets small capital rather than a full allocation.
  5. Funding plan. Shadow-trade for 2–3 months. Then $50M GMV at 4% volatility: about $2M of annual risk, about $126k daily. Ramp to $150M, then $300M, if realized costs stay within 25% of the model, re-fitting impact at each step.
  6. Kill criteria, written first. Hard stop at a drawdown of 1.5× the annual volatility budget ($3M at stage one); review if realized cost runs 50% above model for a month or live P&L stops tracking the backtest replayed on live dates.

Why judge implementation, not P&L, early? At a true Sharpe of 0.75, the chance of losing money over six months is about 30%, over a year about 23% [Estimate] (normal approximation). In simulation, the 1.5× stop trips within a year about 8% of the time at Sharpe 0.75 but only 23% of the time when alpha is zero [Estimate]. Stops limit damage; they are weak detectors of dead strategies. Cost, fill and tracking diagnostics carry the early decision (L1).

Math: the Fundamental Law of Active Management

Grinold's law: information ratio ≈ skill × √(independent bets per year):

\[ IR \approx IC \times \sqrt{BR} \]

where IC (the information coefficient) is the correlation between forecasts and realized returns and BR (breadth) is the number of independent forecasts per year. Clarke, de Silva and Thorley add the transfer coefficient TC, roughly the correlation between the risk-adjusted weights an unconstrained optimizer would hold and those actually held:

\[ IR \approx TC \times IC \times \sqrt{BR} \]

Long-only limits, turnover caps and neutrality constraints push TC below 1; their paper reports realized performance at about 0.3–0.8 of the unconstrained law's prediction [Verified].

Illustration: IC = 0.03 on 500 stocks rebalanced monthly gives BR = 6,000 if bets were independent, so IR ≈ 0.03 × 77 ≈ 2.3; with TC = 0.5, 1.2; if correlation cuts effective breadth to 1,500, 0.58. Breadth counts independent bets, not trades.

Math: why the hurdle is ρ × SR_book

Scale both return streams to unit volatility. The maximum Sharpe of an optimal mix of a book with Sharpe \(S_b\) and a candidate with Sharpe \(S_n\) and correlation \(\rho\) is

\[ S^{*2} = \frac{S_b^2 + S_n^2 - 2\rho S_b S_n}{1-\rho^2} \]

and the optimal risk weight on the candidate is proportional to \(S_n - \rho S_b\). It is positive (the candidate belongs in the book) only when \(S_n > \rho S_b\).

docs.title: Questions to ask
docs.text:
• Basic: What is the edge source, and who is on the other side? Is that Sharpe gross or net, and over what period?
  • Informed: What is the breakeven cost versus realized cost? How correlated is this with the book and with published factors? How many variants did you try?
  • Sharp: What did it do in August 2007, March 2020 or your worst week? At what size does net Sharpe hit your hurdle? 🔒 (exact capacity is usually proprietary) Were the kill criteria written before launch?

docs.title: Analyst revisions and sentiment
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Analysts update slowly and in herds, so consensus estimate revisions are serially correlated and prices drift after them: revision momentum is one of the most durable mid-frequency alphas.
  • Recommendation changes move prices on the day and drift afterwards, especially downgrades, but trading on them is costly.
  • Short interest and days-to-cover read the footprints of informed short sellers; the same crowded shorts are the squeeze candidates.
  • News scores, social-media sentiment and options-implied signals (skew, put-call parity deviations) add fast, crowded information that decays in days.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source informational · behavioral Holding period Days (news, options) to 1–3 months (revisions, short interest) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Investors anchored on stale estimates; attention-driven buyers of heavily discussed names; stock traders slower than informed option buyers. They are not watching continuously, or trade for other reasons. Universe & instruments US stocks with at least three estimates; listed options for implied signals; borrowable names for shorts Data required Point-in-time estimates and recommendations (for example I/B/E/S), short interest, lending utilization and fees, scored news, option implied volatilities Core algorithms used D2 Feature engineering · D3 Signal transforms · D4 Evaluating signals · F5 Alpha combination and ensembling · F4 LLMs and foundation models in quant Infra intensity Overnight batch; real-time feeds for news Capacity (rough $ range) Revisions and short interest: \(1B–\)5B as a component [Estimate]; news and options signals: \(100M–\)1B [Estimate] (decay within days forces high turnover) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Recommendation long-short: >4% a year gross, 1986–1996, not reliably positive after costs [Reported]; option-skew long-short: ~10.9% a year risk-adjusted, gross of costs, 1996–2005 [Reported]; both academic backtests, decayed since. Inside a composite: +0.2–0.5 net Sharpe contribution [Lore] Turnover Revisions 100–400% a year; news sleeves 20–50% a day [Lore] Main risks / failure modes Short squeezes, vendor-signal crowding, back-filled data, regime shifts in analyst behaviour Crowding risk High: revisions and short interest are standard in commercial factor libraries; vendor sentiment is sold to many clients Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, systematic asset managers, multi-manager quant pods Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
Analysts are slow, careful and social: when news arrives, each moves part of the way and watches peers, so one upward revision predicts more. The market under-reacts too, and price follows the revision trail for weeks.

Other signals read who is already acting on information: short sellers are, on average, informed, as are option traders buying puts before bad news. News and social tone is sometimes information and sometimes noise that reverses.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Partial adjustment and herding. Gradual analyst updating makes earnings revisions autocorrelated, and prices drift after them (Givoly & Lakonishok 1979; Stickel 1991) [Reported].
  • Informed footprints. Heavily shorted stocks underperform lightly shorted ones by about 1.16% over the next 20 trading days, risk-adjusted (Boehmer, Jones & Zhang 2008) [Reported]. Informed traders favour options, so skew leads stock prices (Xing, Zhang & Zhao 2010) [Reported].
  • Noise versus news. Tetlock (2007) found media pessimism pushes prices down and then reverses (noise); Tetlock, Saar-Tsechansky & Macskassy (2008) found negative words in firm news predict earnings and returns (information) [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
Signal Construction Horizon Origin Revision momentum (up − down revisions) / analysts, 1–3 months; or Δconsensus / price 1–3 months Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok (1996) Recommendation changes Upgrades, downgrades, initiations Days to months Womack (1996) Days-to-cover Short interest / average daily volume 1–3 months Asquith, Pathak & Ritter (2005) News sentiment Vendor score × relevance × novelty 1–5 days Heston & Sinha (2017) Social sentiment Tone of investor posts and articles Days to months Chen, De, Hu & Hwang (2014) Option skew OTM put IV − ATM call IV 1–4 weeks Xing, Zhang & Zhao (2010); Cremers & Weinbaum (2010)

Then z-score within sector, orthogonalize to surprise and momentum, IC-weight, neutralize and pass to the optimizer.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Revisions (illustrative). Twelve analysts; over 60 days seven raised next-year EPS and one cut. Net revision ratio = (7 − 1) / 12 = 0.50. Consensus moved $4.00 → $4.20 on an $80 stock: revision-to-price = 0.20 / 80 = 0.25%. Within sector these z-score to +1.6 and +1.2; average +1.4.

The short-side trap (illustrative). Days-to-cover = 6M shares short / 0.5M ADV = 12 days, top decile; the model wants to short \(2M. Expected underperformance 1.0% a month = +\)20,000. Borrow fee 25% a year = 2.1% a month = −\(41,700. Net ≈ −\)21,700 a month before squeeze risk: fee-adjusted alpha is what matters.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Feature design: D2; transforms: D3; decay and IC by horizon: D4; blending with other alphas: F5; LLM news scoring: F4; point-in-time estimates: D1.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def revision_signal(est, asof, window_days=60, min_analysts=3):
    """est: detail estimates (ticker, analyst, eps, announce_date), used only if
    announced by `asof` (point-in-time). Returns net up-minus-down share."""
    e = est[(est.announce_date <= asof) &
            (est.announce_date > asof - pd.Timedelta(days=window_days))]
    e = e.sort_values("announce_date")
    e["chg"] = e.groupby(["ticker", "analyst"]).eps.diff()  # simplified: ignores pre-window
    g = e.dropna(subset=["chg"]).groupby("ticker").chg
    net = g.apply(lambda c: (c > 0).sum() - (c < 0).sum()) / g.count()
    return net[g.count() >= min_analysts]

def sentiment_composite(rev, dtc, news, skew, sector):
    """Inputs: Series by ticker. Signs: revisions +, days-to-cover -, news +, skew -."""
    raw = pd.DataFrame({"rev": rev, "dtc": -np.log1p(dtc), "news": news, "skew": -skew})
    z = raw.groupby(sector).transform(lambda c: ((c - c.mean()) / c.std()).clip(-3, 3))
    return z.mean(axis=1, skipna=True)          # equal weight; F5 would IC-weight

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Point-in-time estimates. Ljungqvist, Malloy & Marston (2009) showed historical I/B/E/S recommendation records were altered after the fact [Reported]; use archived snapshots and announcement dates.
  • Hygiene. Drop estimates older than about 90–120 days and strip the post-earnings revision wave that echoes the surprise (earnings).
  • Short-interest timing. Exchange short interest is reported twice monthly with a lag; key it to publication date, not settlement date (shorting).
  • Borrow. Score alpha net of lending fees; cap utilization.
  • News. Deduplicate, require relevance and novelty, trade fast (NLP and LLM signals).

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative $1B GMV sleeve:

Line % of GMV per year Revision momentum +2.5% Short interest and lending +1.5% News and options (fast) +2.0% Trading costs (10% a day at 7 bps) −1.8% Borrow fees on crowded shorts −0.5% Financing spread −0.3% Net +3.4%

At 4% volatility, gross Sharpe ≈ 1.5 and net ≈ 0.85 [Estimate].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok (1996): revisions and earnings surprises predict returns, and price momentum partly reflects earnings momentum [Reported].
  • Womack (1996): downgrade drift lasts about six months, upgrade drift about a month [Reported]. Barber et al. (2001): consensus-recommendation strategies earned >4% gross, gone after costs [Reported].
  • Asquith, Pathak & Ritter (2005): high short interest plus low institutional ownership predicts underperformance [Reported].
  • Chen et al. (2014): Seeking Alpha opinions predict returns and earnings surprises [Reported].
  • Xing, Zhang & Zhao (2010): steepest-smirk stocks underperform by about 10.9% a year (1996–2005) [Reported].
  • McLean & Pontiff (2016): published predictors lose 58% post-publication [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Revisions and short interest sit in every commercial factor library, so standalone returns have shrunk and drawdowns are shared. Vendor news scores reach many clients at once and decay within hours to days [Lore]; edge has moved to proprietary parsing and LLM scoring.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Short squeezes. In January 2021, heavily shorted stocks such as GameStop rose many-fold within days as retail buying, options activity and short covering fed each other [Verified] (SEC staff report, 2021).
  • Rule changes. Regulation FD (effective October 2000) ended selective disclosure to analysts, changing what revisions contain [Verified].
  • Crowding and back-filled data inflate backtests (backtest pitfalls).

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Consensus-mean revisions, monthly deciles (Chan et al. 1996) [Reported] Analyst-level revisions weighted by accuracy and recency [Lore] Short interest ratio Daily lending utilization and fees plus short interest [Lore] Dictionary word counts (Tetlock 2007) [Reported] Vendor scores and LLM classifiers on news and transcripts [Lore]

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Earnings and event-driven, NLP and LLM signals, alternative data (crowd-sourced estimates, web traffic), momentum (earnings momentum's price cousin).

docs.text:

flowchart TD

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Revisions are still working, but only analyst-level." → Consensus revisions are crowded; individual-analyst detail adds edge.
  • "Strip the post-earnings wave." → Remove revisions that merely echo the surprise.
  • "Days-to-cover beats the raw short ratio." → Scaling by volume measures how hard covering is.
  • "It's a good short, but not at that fee." → Borrow cost exceeds expected alpha.
  • "That news score is gone by lunch." → Vendor sentiment decays within hours.
  • "Skew is telling us someone knows something." → Steep put skew precedes bad news.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality Follow the analysts' buy ratings Consensus levels lose to costs; revisions and changes carry the signal High short interest is a free short Borrow fees and squeezes often exceed the alpha Sentiment always means irrationality Some tone is information about earnings, some is noise that reverses

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you use consensus or individual-analyst revisions?
  • How do you timestamp short-interest data?

Informed

  • How do you separate revision alpha from earnings-surprise alpha?
  • Do you score shorts net of borrow fees?
  • How fast does your news signal decay?

Sharp

  • What did January 2021 cost your short-interest sleeve, and what changed? 🔒
  • Which analysts do you up-weight, and how is accuracy measured? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: why revisions are autocorrelated, and signal definitions

Partial adjustment: if each analyst moves a fraction \(\kappa \in (0,1)\) toward the full-information forecast \(E_t\),

\[ F_t = F_{t-1} + \kappa \left(E_t - F_{t-1}\right) , \]

then after a one-time shock to \(E\), revisions \(F_t - F_{t-1}\) shrink geometrically by \((1-\kappa)\) but keep the same sign: today's revision predicts tomorrow's.

Days-to-cover and option skew:

\[ DTC_i = \frac{\text{shares short}_i}{\text{ADV}_i}, \qquad SKEW_i = IV^{put}_{OTM,i} - IV^{call}_{ATM,i} . \]

docs.title: Cross-sectional alpha and neutralization
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The canonical mid-frequency quant equity book ranks 1,000–3,000 US stocks against each other every day on many weak signals ("alphas") and holds the top against the bottom for days to weeks, with near-zero market exposure.
  • The pipeline: raw alphas → transforms (winsorize, rank or z-score) → neutralization (regress out beta, industries, styles) → combination → risk model → optimizer with a cost model → trades.
  • The Fundamental Law (IR ≈ TC · IC · √breadth) explains the design: each alpha is barely better than a coin flip (IC 0.01–0.05), so the edge comes from many nearly independent bets.
  • It fails through costs (turnover of 10–40% of the book per day), crowding (August 2007) and decay of known signals.

Level: Core · Read time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source behavioral · informational (plus liquidity provision for reversal-type alphas) Holding period 1–20 trading days Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Benchmarked funds rebalancing to an index, institutions paying for immediacy on large orders, investors who under-react to news. They accept a few bps of leakage per trade because their objective (tracking, liquidity, a multi-year thesis) dominates. Universe & instruments US common stocks above a liquidity floor, long and short in cash or swaps; index futures to hedge residual beta Data required Point-in-time prices, corporate actions, fundamentals, estimates; industry codes; a factor risk model; spread, ADV and volatility for costs; borrow fees Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · D4 Evaluating signals · F5 Alpha combination and ensembling · P1 Risk models · P3 Mean-variance optimization · P5 Transaction cost and impact models Infra intensity Low latency sensitivity; heavy batch research compute; seconds per optimizer solve Capacity (rough $ range) \(1B–\)10B gross market value (GMV) per book [Estimate] (square-root impact: total cost grows like size^1.5, alpha like size) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Diversified multi-alpha book: gross 1.5–3, net 1–2 [Lore] (practitioner estimates, 2010s–2020s; no audited disclosure). Single published anomalies are weaker and lose ~58% of in-sample return after publication [Verified] (McLean & Pontiff 2016) Turnover 10–40% of GMV per day [Lore] (about 25–100× per year) Main risks / failure modes Crowded deleveraging, cost-model error, factor leakage, alpha decay, look-ahead, short squeezes Crowding risk High: shared data (Compustat, I/B/E/S), similar transforms and commercial risk models Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, multi-manager quant pods, alpha-research platforms; WorldQuant stated that 80 of the 101 alphas in Kakushadze (2016) were in production when published [Verified] Lab Lab 11

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
A cross-sectional book never asks "will the market go up?" It asks "which of these 2,000 stocks will beat the others over the next week?" If every stock falls 3% tomorrow, a well-built book should barely notice.

Each alpha is a weak opinion: "analysts just raised estimates", "fell hard last week", "low accruals". Each is right perhaps 51–52% of the time. Hold hundreds of names per side and the coin flips average out.

Neutralization makes sure each flip is about what you think. If your "cheap stocks" list is 60% banks, you are betting on banks, not cheapness. Neutralization removes the bank bet (and the market and small-cap bets), leaving the stock-specific part the alpha was meant to capture.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
1. Behavioral under-reaction. Investors digest earnings news, revisions and accounting quality slowly; prices drift toward the news (see earnings and revisions).
  2. Liquidity provision. Reversal alphas are paid for absorbing temporary order imbalances (see short-term reversal).
  3. Residual risk premia. Some signals earn pay for risks your model omits; neutralization deliberately removes most known premia.

Arbitrage stays limited because shorting is costly, capital is finite and every dollar of alpha must clear a cost hurdle.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Universe: point-in-time membership and a liquidity floor (D1).
  2. Raw alphas: one number per stock per day (D2).
  3. Transform: winsorize, then rank or z-score across stocks each date.
  4. Neutralize: regress on beta, industry dummies and style exposures; keep the residual.
  5. Evaluate and combine: information coefficient, decay, turnover; blend into one forecast.
  6. Scale: alpha = IC × residual volatility × score (Grinold).
  7. Optimize with risk, cost and constraints; trade part of the way to target.
  8. Execute (VWAP/IS, closing auction) and attribute P&L next morning.
flowchart LR
    U["Universe<br/>(PIT, liquid)"] --> A["Raw alphas"]
    A --> T["Transforms<br/>winsorize, rank"]
    T --> N["Neutralize<br/>beta, industry, style"]
    N --> C["Combine<br/>IC-weighted, ridge, ML"]
    C --> R["Risk and<br/>cost models"]
    R --> O["Optimizer"]
    O --> X["Execution"]
    X --> P["P&L attribution"]
    P -.->|"decay, IC drift"| A

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
A. Neutralization (illustrative). Four stocks, two sectors, one raw z-scored signal:

Stock Sector Beta Raw z Sector mean Sector-neutral A Semis 1.4 +1.5 +1.0 +0.5 B Semis 1.3 +0.5 +1.0 −0.5 C Banks 1.1 −0.3 −1.0 +0.7 D Banks 0.9 −1.7 −1.0 −0.7

The raw signal is mostly "long semis, short banks". Sector-neutral, the book is long A and C, short B and D. At \(100M GMV (\)41.7M per unit of score): A +\(20.8M, C +\)29.2M, B −\(20.8M, D −\)29.2M. Net beta dollars: 20.8×1.4 + 29.2×1.1 − 20.8×1.3 − 29.2×0.9 = +\(7.9M, so a 2% market drop costs ~\)158k. Sector-neutral is not beta-neutral: add beta to the regression or hedge with ~$7.9M of index futures.

B. Dollar- vs beta-neutral (illustrative). $500M long at beta 0.8 against \(500M short at beta 1.2 is dollar-neutral but carries −\)200M of beta: a +1% market day loses ~$2M.

C. Fundamental Law (illustrative). IC 0.03, 2,000 stocks, 5-day horizon (≈ 50 periods a year): nominal breadth 100,000, √ ≈ 316, IR ≈ 9.5; with a transfer coefficient of 0.4, 3.8. If correlated residuals and overlapping holds leave 10% of bets truly independent, √10,000 = 100 and IR ≈ 0.03 × 100 × 0.4 = 1.2, where real books live.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Transforms and IC: D3, D4. Combination: F5. Risk model: P1, P2. Optimizer and costs: P3, P5, P6. Lab 11 implements the transforms and IC diagnostics on synthetic data.

import numpy as np

def zscore(x, clip=3.0):
    """Cross-sectional z-score on one date, winsorized at +/- clip sigma."""
    z = (x - np.nanmean(x)) / np.nanstd(x)
    return np.clip(z, -clip, clip)

def neutralize(signal, exposures):
    """Residual after least-squares regression of the signal on exposures.
    exposures: N x K (beta column, industry dummies, style z-scores)."""
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(exposures, signal, rcond=None)
    return signal - exposures @ coef        # orthogonal to every exposure column

def daily_forecast(raw_alphas, exposures, ic, resid_vol, ic_combo=0.04):
    """raw_alphas: {name: N-vector}; ic: {name: trailing rank IC}; returns daily alpha."""
    combo = np.zeros(len(resid_vol))
    for name, x in raw_alphas.items():
        s = neutralize(zscore(x), exposures)
        combo += max(ic[name], 0.0) * s / np.std(s)   # IC-weighted; ignores alpha correlations
    score = neutralize(zscore(combo), exposures)      # re-neutralize after winsorizing
    return ic_combo * resid_vol * score              # Grinold: alpha = IC * vol * score
# Names follow Lab 11 (zscore, neutralize); simplified: no NaN handling, unweighted regression.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Rank vs z-score. Ranks resist outliers but discard magnitude; z-scores keep it but need winsorizing.
  • What to neutralize. Beta and industries always; styles (size, value, momentum, volatility) usually. Over-neutralizing deletes alpha correlated with a factor.
  • Signal vs optimizer. If the alpha has parts the risk model cannot "see", the optimizer over-loads on them (Ceria, Saxena & Stubbs 2012, "factor alignment").
  • Weighted regression (for example by √market cap) stops tiny names dominating.
  • Trade toward the aim: move a fraction of the way to target daily (Gârleanu & Pedersen 2013).
  • Execution and borrow: participation caps of 1–5% of ADV [Lore]; hard-to-borrow names penalized (shorting and financing).

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative: \(1B GMV, turnover 15% per day (\)37.8B traded per year).

Line $M per year % of GMV Residual alpha captured +80.0 +8.0% Factor P&L (leakage) ≈ 0 expected, ±10 realized ≈ 0 Half-spread (3 bps traded) −11.3 −1.1% Market impact (4 bps) −15.1 −1.5% Commissions and fees (1 bp) −3.8 −0.4% Borrow (0.4% on $500M short) −2.0 −0.2% Financing spread, net −3.0 −0.3% Net +44.8 +4.5%

At 4% annualized volatility on GMV, gross Sharpe ≈ 2.0 and net ≈ 1.1: costs take 44% of gross alpha [Estimate].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Kakushadze (2016) published 101 real-life trading alphas with average holding periods of about 0.6–6.4 days and average pairwise correlation of 15.9% [Verified]; low correlation is what makes breadth across alphas valuable.
  • McLean & Pontiff (2016): across 97 predictors, returns are 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower post-publication [Verified].
  • Grinold (1989) derived IR ≈ IC·√breadth; Clarke, de Silva & Thorley (2002) added the transfer coefficient and showed constraints shrink realized IR [Verified].
  • Daily rank ICs of 0.01–0.05 per alpha are the practitioner norm; above 0.1 on a large universe usually means a bug [Lore].
  • Tulchinsky et al. (Finding Alphas) and Isichenko (2021) describe this pipeline at industrial scale [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text:
Capacity. Under square-root impact, doubling the book raises impact per dollar ~41%. In the table, a $4B book pays ~8 bps impact and ~12 bps all-in, about 4.5% of GMV a year, unless it slows down and drops its fastest alphas [Estimate].

Crowding. Shared vendors, academic signals and risk models make residual books overlap; one forced seller hurts all (see the diagram).

Decay. Known alphas lose about half their return (McLean & Pontiff); research must keep replacing them (L2).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• August 2007. Over 7–9 August many quant equity funds lost heavily at once, then partly rebounded on 10 August; Khandani & Lo (2007, 2011) attribute it to the rapid unwind of large market-neutral portfolios [Verified].
  • Factor leakage. Imperfect neutralization leaves hidden style bets, exposed in the 2018–2020 value drawdown (see quant winters).
  • Short squeezes. In January 2021, heavily shorted stocks spiked on retail buying and short covering [Verified] (SEC staff report, 2021).
  • Backtest bias and underestimated impact (V3).

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today One alpha into mean-variance Hundreds to thousands of alphas, combined by regularized regression or ML (Kakushadze 2016; Tulchinsky et al.) [Reported] IR = IC·√N, independent bets Effective breadth far below nominal, backed out from realized IR [Lore] One commercial risk model Proprietary or statistical models to trade, commercial ones for limits [Lore] Rebalance fully Partial, cost-aware trading toward an aim (Gârleanu & Pedersen 2013) [Verified]

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text:
• Factor-residual mean reversion: the residual's reversion is the alpha.
  • Fundamental quant signals, earnings, revisions and sentiment: alpha families that feed this book.
  • Factor investing: the long-only, un-neutralized, low-turnover cousin.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
The crowding loop behind August 2007:

flowchart TD
    S["Large fund de-risks"] --> L["Sells longs, covers shorts"]
    L --> M["Common longs fall,<br/>common shorts rise"]
    M --> Q["Overlapping quant books lose"]
    Q --> V["Risk limits breached"]
    V --> D["They de-lever too"]
    D --> L
    M --> F["Index barely moves:<br/>the damage is residual"]

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Neutralize to industry and the Barra styles before you look at the IC." → Otherwise the IC partly measures factor returns.
  • "That alpha is short-vol in disguise." → It loads on low volatility; neutralized, little remains.
  • "Our effective breadth is a few hundred bets a year." → Correlated bets shrink the √N.
  • "The TC on that book is terrible." → Constraints stop holdings reflecting the forecast.
  • "IC is 2%, but it's a 1-day signal and costs eat it." → Real but unusable at that turnover.
  • "We trade a third of the way to target each day." → Partial adjustment balancing decay against impact.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality Market-neutral means riskless It removes beta, not factor, crowding or squeeze risk Higher IC is always better IC 0.05 at 80% daily turnover can lose to IC 0.02 at 5% after costs More neutralization is safer It can delete real alpha and create exposures the model cannot see

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you neutralize at the signal level, in the optimizer, or both?
  • Dollar-neutral, beta-neutral or both?

Informed

  • How far is effective breadth from nominal?
  • Which constraint costs the most transfer coefficient?
  • How do you set the trade-toward-target rate per alpha half-life?

Sharp

  • How did the book behave on 7–9 August 2007, and what changed afterwards?
  • How much residual return does your statistical risk model explain that the commercial one misses? 🔒
  • What is the IC half-life of a newly added alpha in production? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: residualization, the Fundamental Law and alpha scaling

Neutralization as projection. Signal \(s\), exposures \(X\) (\(N \times K\)), weights \(W\):

\[ s_\perp = \left(I - X (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W\right) s, \qquad X^\top W s_\perp = 0 . \]

Sector-demeaning is the case where \(X\) holds only industry dummies and \(W = I\). Beta-neutral holdings satisfy \(\beta^\top h = 0\); dollar-neutral, \(\mathbf{1}^\top h = 0\).

Fundamental Law (Grinold 1989; Clarke, de Silva & Thorley 2002), with \(BR\) the number of independent forecasts per year:

\[ IR \approx TC \cdot IC \cdot \sqrt{BR} . \]

Alpha scaling (Grinold and Kahn), score \(z_i\), residual volatility \(\omega_i\):

\[ \alpha_i = IC \cdot \omega_i \cdot z_i . \]

With \(IC = 0.03\), \(\omega = 30\%\) and \(z = 2\): 1.8% a year, which is why costs dominate.

docs.title: Earnings and event-driven
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Earnings releases are a stock's biggest scheduled information events; the classic quant trade is post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD): buy positive surprises, short negative ones, hold for weeks.
  • Bernard & Thomas (1989): about 4.2% over 60 trading days for top-minus-bottom surprise deciles (1974–1985). Martineau (2022): gone in non-microcaps since 2006. 2025 papers dispute it; the question is open.
  • Neighbouring event alphas: the earnings-announcement premium, pre-announcement liquidity reversal, guidance changes, and merger arbitrage (a short put on deal completion).
  • Execution is the hard part: gaps and event-day spreads eat much of a thin edge.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source behavioral · liquidity provision (plus a risk premium in merger arbitrage) Holding period 1–60 trading days after the event; merger arbitrage holds until deal close (months) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Inattentive investors who under-react on busy days and Fridays; impatient traders needing liquidity before announcements; target holders who sell rather than bear deal-break risk Universe & instruments US stocks with scheduled earnings; merger targets and acquirers; options for event-volatility variants Data required Point-in-time release timestamps, actuals and consensus (for example I/B/E/S), guidance, intraday prices; deal terms Core algorithms used D1 Point-in-time data and cleaning · D2 Feature engineering · D4 Evaluating signals · V3 Backtest pitfalls · E5 Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos Infra intensity Moderate: minutes matter for the reaction, days for drift Capacity (rough $ range) \(100M–\)2B for standalone PEAD [Estimate] (drift is concentrated in small, illiquid names and entries cluster on high-cost days) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) PEAD: ~4.2% per 60 days top-minus-bottom decile, gross, 1974–1985 academic backtest [Reported]; near zero in non-microcaps since 2006 [Verified] (Martineau 2022), contested. Merger arbitrage: ~4% a year excess return, 1963–1998 academic study [Reported] Turnover High and lumpy: positions open after each event and roll off within weeks Main risks / failure modes Overnight gaps, guidance shocks, stale consensus, timestamp errors, deal breaks Crowding risk High: everyone has the same consensus feed and the same SUE formula Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, event-driven pods at multi-manager firms, merger-arbitrage funds Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: Earnings are a quarterly exam. The market grades it within seconds but historically took weeks to finish: beats kept drifting up, misses kept drifting down. A quant needs not why a company beat but by how much, relative to how noisy its surprises usually are, and a way to trade after the first reaction without paying it all away in spreads.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Limited attention. Responses are weaker and drift stronger for Friday announcements (DellaVigna & Pollet 2009) and on days crowded with other announcements (Hirshleifer, Lim & Teoh 2009) [Reported].
  • Misread persistence. Bernard & Thomas (1990): prices act as if earnings were a random walk although seasonal changes are autocorrelated, so much of the drift lands at the next announcements [Reported].
  • Liquidity provision. Short-term reversals are much larger just before announcements, when liquidity providers demand more (So & Wang 2014) [Reported].
  • Risk. Announcement months earn higher returns, read as systematic risk (Savor & Wilson 2016) or attention-driven buying (Frazzini & Lamont 2007) [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Keep a point-in-time calendar of confirmed dates and times.
  2. At release, compute standardized unexpected earnings (SUE): surprise scaled by the stock's usual surprise size; add revenue surprise.
  3. Rank against other recent announcers within sector.
  4. Enter after the gap over one to three sessions (VWAP, closing auction).
  5. Hold 20–60 days with decaying weight; neutralize beta and industry.
  6. Decide whether to hold through the next announcement.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
PEAD (illustrative). EPS $1.20 against consensus $1.05; past surprises have a standard deviation of $0.10, so SUE = 0.15 / 0.10 = 1.5 (top decile). The stock gaps +6% at the open. Buy $5M over two days.

Line If drift exists If it does not Drift capture (+2% of $5M) +$100,000 $0 Entry: 10 bps spread + 15 bps impact on event days −$12,500 −$12,500 Exit: 10 bps −$5,000 −$5,000 Net +$82,500 −$17,500

The 2% is one leg's half of the historical 4.2% spread; whether it survives in large caps decides the trade.

Merger arbitrage (illustrative). Cash offer $50; target trades at $47.50; expected close in six months; estimated break price $38. Spread = 2.50 / 47.50 = 5.3% (≈ 10.8% annualized). Market-implied completion probability, ignoring discounting: (47.50 − 38) / (50 − 38) = 79%. Payoff: +5.3% if it closes, −20% if it breaks, the shape of a short put.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Timestamps come from D1; surprise features from D2; drift curves and IC by horizon from D4; timing look-ahead from V3; event-day execution from E5.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def sue(actual_eps, consensus_eps, past_surprises, min_hist=4):
    """Standardized unexpected earnings (analyst-consensus version)."""
    if len(past_surprises) < min_hist:
        return np.nan
    scale = max(np.std(past_surprises), 0.01)       # floor avoids dividing by ~0
    return (actual_eps - consensus_eps) / scale

def pead_weights(events, today, hold_days=40, entry_lag=1, half_life=20):
    """events: DataFrame(ticker, ann_ts, sue, sector); ages in calendar days.
    Enter only on the first full session after the release (never the pre-release close)."""
    age = (today - events.ann_ts).dt.days
    live = events[(age >= entry_lag) & (age <= hold_days)].set_index("ticker")
    score = live.groupby("sector").sue.rank(pct=True) - 0.5       # sector-relative
    w = score * 0.5 ** ((today - live.ann_ts).dt.days / half_life)  # decay with age
    return (w - w.mean()) / (w - w.mean()).abs().sum()            # dollar-neutral, gross 1

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Timestamps. An after-close release cannot trade at that day's close.
  • Consensus hygiene. Stale estimates and GAAP versus "street" EPS change SUE; analyst-based SUE drifts more than time-series SUE (Livnat & Mendenhall 2006) [Reported].
  • More than EPS. Revenue surprises and guidance add information (Jegadeesh & Livnat 2006) [Reported].
  • Liquidity. Event-day spreads are wide [Lore]; spreading entry over days and using the close cuts costs.
  • Index events follow the same logic with flows: see flow-driven strategies.

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative large-cap PEAD book, \(500M GMV, ~30-day holds (\)8.4B traded per year):

Line % of GMV per year Drift capture +3.0% Announcement-premium tilt +0.5% Spread and impact at event liquidity (12 bps) −2.0% Borrow and financing −0.5% Net +1.0%

At 4% volatility, net Sharpe ≈ 0.25 [Estimate]: thin, which is why most firms run SUE as one input to a multi-alpha book rather than standalone.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Ball & Brown (1968) first documented drift; Bernard & Thomas (1989): ~4.2% top-minus-bottom over 60 days, positive in 41 of 48 quarters, 1974–1985 [Reported].
  • Chordia et al. (2009): drift concentrates in illiquid stocks; costs absorb most paper profits [Reported].
  • Martineau (2022): no drift in large stocks since 2006, recently none in microcaps; prices now absorb surprises on the day [Verified].
  • Subrahmanyam (2025) notes two 2025 papers reporting strong PEAD (t-statistics above 14) and attributes the disagreement to research design [Reported]. Evidence is mixed; no verdict here.
  • Mitchell & Pulvino (2001): merger arbitrage earned ~4% a year excess, with returns resembling short index puts in down markets [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Drift lives where costs are highest, so capacity is small. Decay is central: the reaction moved into the first minutes, shifting edge to whoever parses releases and calls fastest (NLP and LLM signals).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Gap risk. On 3 February 2022 Meta fell roughly a quarter in one session after earnings [Reported].
  • Deal breaks. In October 2014 AbbVie walked away from Shire after US anti-inversion rules changed, inflicting heavy losses on arbitrageurs [Reported].
  • Timing bugs. Misdated releases create fictitious backtest drift.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Time-series SUE, quarterly deciles (Bernard & Thomas 1989) [Reported] Consensus SUE plus revenue, guidance and call text, sector-neutral [Lore] Hold 60 days Hold until the measured drift decays, often shorter in large caps (Martineau 2022) [Verified] Trade at the announcement close Enter after the gap with auction and VWAP algos [Lore]

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Merger arbitrage, flow-driven index events, guidance and negative pre-announcements, post-release analyst revisions, options event volatility (volatility risk premium).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We don't trade the print, we trade the day after." → Enter after the gap to avoid event-day costs.
  • "SUE alone is a commodity." → Everyone has it; edge comes from extra features or speed.
  • "PEAD's a small-cap story now." → Drift survives, if anywhere, where it is costly to trade.
  • "The arb spread is pricing about an 80% close." → Market-implied deal probability.
  • "Don't hold through the next print without a view." → Gap risk resets each quarter.
  • "Watch the late reporters." → Unexpected delays to a release date often precede bad news.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality PEAD is a free lunch Largely gone in large caps since 2006, and costly where it remains Merger arbitrage is low risk It is a short put: steady small gains, rare large losses Faster is always better For drift, waiting a day often beats event-day spreads

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you use consensus or time-series surprises?
  • When do you enter relative to the release?

Informed

  • How has your measured drift by size bucket changed since 2006?

Sharp

  • Do you hold through the next announcement, and what does that add? 🔒
  • What share of event P&L arrives in the first hour versus the drift window? 🔒
  • How do you size merger arbitrage against correlated deal breaks?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: SUE and implied deal probability

Standardized unexpected earnings, with consensus \(F_{t}\) and the standard deviation of the last \(k\) surprises:

\[ SUE_{t} = \frac{EPS_{t} - F_{t}}{\sigma\left(EPS_{t-j} - F_{t-j}\right)_{j=1..k}} . \]

Implied completion probability with discount rate \(r\) and time to close \(T\):

\[ P_0 = \frac{p \, O + (1-p) \, B}{(1+r)^{T}} \;\Rightarrow\; p = \frac{P_0 (1+r)^{T} - B}{O - B} . \]

docs.title: Fundamental quant signals
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Fundamental quant turns financial-statement judgments (is it cheap? are earnings backed by cash? is management over-investing?) into ratios computed identically for 3,000 stocks and ranked within sector.
  • The core families: value (B/M, E/P, EV/EBITDA), profitability (gross profits / assets), accruals, asset growth, and earnings-quality composites.
  • The hard part is the data, not the ratio: point-in-time availability, reporting lags and restatements decide whether a backtest is honest.
  • Slow, cheap to trade and high capacity, but crowded and decayed: accruals largely faded, and published predictors lose about half their return.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source risk premium · behavioral Holding period 1–12 months (inputs update quarterly) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Investors who extrapolate growth and fixate on headline earnings rather than their cash content; insofar as value and investment are risk premia, anyone avoiding that risk Universe & instruments US stocks with statement coverage; financials and utilities often excluded or scored separately Data required Point-in-time fundamentals with filing dates (vendor PIT archives or SEC XBRL), prices, estimates, industry codes Core algorithms used D1 Point-in-time data and cleaning · D2 Feature engineering · D3 Signal transforms · D4 Evaluating signals · P1 Risk models Infra intensity Negligible latency sensitivity; data engineering is the main cost Capacity (rough $ range) \(1B–\)20B+ per strategy [Estimate] (turnover ~1–3× a year versus 25–100× for daily books, so impact per dollar of alpha is an order of magnitude lower) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Single academic long-short factors (value, profitability, investment): gross roughly 0.3–0.5 over 1963–2020s, weaker post-publication [Estimate]; diversified sector-neutral composite: net 0.5–1.0 [Lore] Turnover 100–300% of GMV per year [Lore] Main risks / failure modes Long value drawdowns, junk rallies, look-ahead in data, sector concentration Crowding risk High: same Compustat fields and the same papers everywhere Firm types that run it Systematic asset managers, quant hedge funds, "quantamental" teams, smart-beta index providers (long-only versions) Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A fundamental analyst reads one 10-K deeply; a fundamental quant reads 3,000 shallowly but identically. Each diligence judgment (cheap versus peers? earnings converting to cash? balance sheet bloating through acquisitions?) becomes a ratio ranked within its industry daily, and breadth does the rest.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Two explanations compete, and both have evidence:

  • Risk. The clean-surplus valuation identity says that, at a given price-to-book, higher expected profitability implies a higher expected return and higher expected investment a lower one; Fama & French (2015) built their profitability (RMW) and investment (CMA) factors on this logic [Verified].
  • Mispricing. Sloan (1996) argued investors fixate on reported earnings and miss that accrual-heavy earnings persist less than cash earnings [Reported]. Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008) read the asset-growth effect as over-extrapolation of growth [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Build a point-in-time panel: every value stamped with the date it became public.
  2. Compute ratios from trailing-twelve-month flows and latest balances.
  3. Winsorize and z-score within industry; banks' book-to-market is not comparable to software's.
  4. Combine into a composite; neutralize to beta, industry and size.
  5. Feed it to the cross-sectional book as a slow alpha, or rebalance standalone monthly.
Signal Construction Sign Origin Value Book equity / market cap; earnings / price; EBITDA / EV + Fama & French (1992); Loughran & Wellman (2011) Profitability (Revenue − COGS) / total assets + Novy-Marx (2013) Accruals (Net income − operating cash flow) / average assets − Sloan (1996) Asset growth Year-over-year change in total assets − Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008) Quality composites Piotroski F-score, quality-minus-junk + Piotroski (2000); Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2019)

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: two semiconductor-equipment firms, same price and same trailing earnings of $100M.

Item ($M) Firm X Firm Y Net income 100 100 Operating cash flow 40 130 Average total assets 1,000 1,000 Accruals / assets (100 − 40)/1,000 = +6.0% (100 − 130)/1,000 = −3.0% Revenue − COGS 320 300 Gross profitability 32% 30% Total assets, now vs a year ago 1,000 vs 800 1,000 vs 950 Asset growth +25% +5.3%

Same E/P, different quality. Suppose within-sector z-scores are X: value 0, profitability +0.3, accruals −1.2 (sign flipped), asset growth −1.5; Y: 0, +0.1, +0.6, +0.2. Equal-weight composites: X = −0.60, Y = +0.23. With a monthly IC of 0.03, residual volatility of 7% a month and Grinold's alpha = IC × vol × score, the forecast spread is 0.03 × 7% × 0.83 ≈ 17 bps per month: tiny per name, which is why it needs breadth.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Point-in-time handling is D1; ratio design D2; sector-relative transforms D3; IC and decay D4; factor exposures P1.

import pandas as pd

def pit_snapshot(filings, asof, lag_days=1):
    """filings: DataFrame(ticker, item, value, filed_date) with values AS FIRST REPORTED.
    Returns the latest value per (ticker, item) that was public on date `asof`."""
    public = filings[filings.filed_date + pd.Timedelta(days=lag_days) <= asof]
    return (public.sort_values("filed_date")
                  .groupby(["ticker", "item"]).value.last().unstack("item"))

def sector_z(col):
    col = col.clip(col.quantile(0.01), col.quantile(0.99))   # winsorize 1%/99%
    return (col - col.mean()) / col.std()

def fundamental_composite(s, mcap, sector):
    """s: pit_snapshot output (TTM flows, latest balances); higher score = buy."""
    raw = pd.DataFrame({
        "value":   s.book_equity / mcap,                          # B/M
        "gp":      (s.revenue - s.cogs) / s.total_assets,           # Novy-Marx
        "accrual": -(s.net_income - s.cfo) / s.total_assets,        # Sloan, sign flipped
        "invest":  -(s.total_assets / s.total_assets_lag - 1),      # asset growth, flipped
    })
    return raw.groupby(sector).transform(sector_z).mean(axis=1)  # then neutralize (D3)

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Reporting lags. 10-Ks are due 60, 75 or 90 days after fiscal year-end and 10-Qs 40 or 45 days after quarter-end, depending on filer size [Verified]. Academic tests often assume a six-month lag; practitioners use the actual filing or announcement timestamp.
  • Announcement vs filing. The release carries income-statement items; the cash-flow statement needed for accruals often arrives only with the 10-Q [Lore]. Timestamp items separately.
  • Restatements. "As-restated" databases overwrite originals with numbers nobody knew then; use values as first reported.
  • Survivorship. Keep delisted firms and delisting returns.
  • Sector-relative and sign-safe. Use E/P, not P/E, so losses rank smoothly; use sector-specific metrics (tangible book for banks).

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative: \(1B GMV sector-neutral composite, turnover 200% a year (\)2B traded).

Line $M per year % of GMV Residual alpha captured +40.0 +4.0% Factor P&L (value, quality tilt not neutralized) ±15 realized ≈ 0 expected Trading costs (15 bps × $2B) −3.0 −0.3% Borrow (0.4% on $500M short) −2.0 −0.2% Financing spread, net −3.0 −0.3% Net +32.0 +3.2%

At 4% volatility, gross Sharpe ≈ 1.0, net ≈ 0.8; factor drawdowns, not costs, are the big risk [Estimate].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Novy-Marx (2013): gross profits-to-assets predicts returns about as well as book-to-market and improves value strategies [Verified].
  • Sloan (1996): low-minus-high accrual hedge earned 10.4% size-adjusted in the following year, 1962–1991 [Reported]; Green, Hand & Soliman (2011): the anomaly decayed until no longer reliably positive, plausibly due to hedge-fund capital [Verified].
  • Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008): low-minus-high asset growth earned about 20% a year in their sample, smaller value-weighted [Reported].
  • McLean & Pontiff (2016): 97 predictors lose 26% out-of-sample and 58% post-publication [Verified].
  • Hou, Xue & Zhang (2020): most of 452 anomalies fail once microcaps are controlled for [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Low turnover gives large capacity, but everyone sees the same Compustat fields, so value, quality and investment are among the most crowded quant trades. Decay is steepest for simple published ratios; composites, sector-specific metrics and XBRL parsed at filing time hold up better [Lore].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Value drawdowns. Value lost badly in 2018–2020 (see quant winters).
  • Junk rallies. Rebounds in unprofitable growth stocks punish quality and investment shorts.
  • Look-ahead. As-restated data or period-end dating can manufacture a Sharpe (V3).

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Annual June sorts, six-month lag (Fama & French 1992) [Reported] Daily updates keyed to actual filing timestamps [Lore] Decile long-short, one ratio Sector-relative composites inside a multi-alpha optimizer [Lore] Book equity as given Adjustments for intangibles, buybacks and industry accounting [Lore]

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Is that point-in-time or as-restated?" → Were values known on the trade date?
  • "We score it within GICS industry." → Ratios are compared only to peers.
  • "Accruals is dead as a standalone." → Decayed, but still useful inside a composite.
  • "Our value leg is really a junk-avoidance leg now." → Returns come more from shorting poor quality than from buying cheap.
  • "Profitability rescued our value sleeve." → Pairing cheap with profitable (Novy-Marx 2013).
  • "Lag everything to the filing timestamp plus a day." → Conservative timing to avoid look-ahead.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality Quants ignore fundamentals Statement data is a core input to most equity quant books A great backtest on value proves it works Without PIT data and delisting returns, it may be look-ahead Published anomalies stay profitable They lose roughly half their return (McLean & Pontiff 2016)

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you use as-first-reported data, and how do you timestamp items?
  • Do you score within sector or neutralize afterwards?

Informed

  • How did your composite behave in the 2018–2020 value drawdown?
  • Do you adjust book equity for intangibles?

Sharp

  • What share of your fundamental alpha survives full factor neutralization? 🔒
  • Which accounting items do you parse from XBRL before vendors update? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the valuation identity behind profitability and investment

Dividend discount with clean-surplus accounting (\(D_t = Y_t - \Delta B_t\), earnings \(Y\), book equity \(B\)):

\[ \frac{M_t}{B_t} = \frac{\sum_{\tau \ge 1} \mathbb{E}\left[Y_{t+\tau} - \Delta B_{t+\tau}\right] / (1+r)^{\tau}}{B_t} . \]

At fixed \(M/B\), higher expected earnings imply higher \(r\); higher expected investment \(\Delta B\), lower \(r\) (Fama & French 2015).

Cash-flow-statement accruals scaled by average total assets \(A\):

\[ \text{Accruals}_t = \frac{NI_t - CFO_t}{(A_t + A_{t-1})/2} . \]

docs.title: Algorithms: overview
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • This module covers the concrete methods inside a quant firm's pipeline: 39 algorithm cards in seven sections (A–G), three overview pages and four end-to-end walkthroughs (H).
  • Start with There is no single algorithm, then use the algorithm map to find any card by its ID.
  • Every card has the same shape: a header table you can skim in 30 seconds, then intuition, pseudocode of 40 lines or fewer, a worked example, practitioner tweaks, failure modes and questions to ask.
  • Twenty runnable Python labs on synthetic data back the cards. The walkthroughs stitch the cards together using the labs' numbers.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: What this module covers
docs.text:
Strategies explains what quant firms trade and why it pays. This module explains how they do it. Each card covers one method (a risk model, a VWAP algorithm, a quoting rule) in enough depth that you can follow a quant's description of it, read its pseudocode, and ask where it breaks. Cards link to the strategies that use them, and the strategy x algorithm matrix shows the full mapping.

docs.title: The eight sections
docs.text: Section Cards The question it answers A. Data and signals D1–D4 Is the data honest, and does this signal predict anything? B. Forecasting models F1–F6 How do many signals become one expected return per stock? C. Validation and backtesting V1–V4 Is the backtest telling the truth? D. Portfolio construction P1–P7 Given forecasts, risk and costs, what should we hold? E. Execution algorithms E1–E6 How do we get there without moving the price? F. Market making and HFT M1–M9 Where should we quote, and how do we avoid being picked off? G. Live trading L1–L3 Is it still working, and when do we retire it? H. End-to-end walkthroughs 4 walkthroughs How do the cards fit together on real numbers?

docs.title: How to read an algorithm card
docs.text:
The line under the title gives three labels. Level is Core (on the main reading path) or Deep dive (optional). Pipeline stage is one of data, signal, forecast, validation, portfolio, execution, market making or live. Last verified is the month of the last fact check. Next comes the header table:

Field What it tells you Purpose (the question it answers) Why the method exists. If you remember one line, remember this one. Inputs → Outputs What it consumes and produces, which is how it plugs into its neighbours on the map. Used by strategies Dossiers that rely on it materially. The matrix is generated from these links. Latency / compute regime Nanoseconds, microseconds, milliseconds, seconds or overnight batch. This sets the kind of engineering it needs. Key parameters The knobs and their typical ranges, so you can tell a sensible setting from a strange one. Main failure modes How it breaks in production. Usually the best thing to talk about. Lab The runnable lab, or "—".

The body always runs in the same order. It starts with intuition and a diagram that highlights the card's place in the pipeline. Then come the algorithm itself (plain steps, then commented pseudocode matching the lab code), a worked example with numbers, and how practitioners tune the parameters. The "textbook vs practice" section sources or tags every claim. After that: how to tell whether the method is working, its failure modes, sample practitioner sentences with glosses, and questions to ask, ordered basic to sharp, with 🔒 marking proprietary territory. Math sits in a collapsed block at the end. Confidence tags ([Verified], [Reported], [Estimate], [Lore]) are explained on the home page.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
Each lab is a short, deterministic Python script on synthetic data, so it shows mechanisms rather than real alpha. Its pseudocode in the cards uses the same names and parameters as the lab.

Lab Cards it supports Also supports 01 Matching engine and order book M6 The limit order book 02 Microprice and fair value M2 — 03 Order-flow imbalance M3 — 04 Markout analysis M5 Equity market making 05 Avellaneda-Stoikov and GLFT quoting M4 Equity market making 06 Options MM and delta hedging M8, M7 Options market making 07 ETF NAV arbitrage — ETF market making, ETF and index arbitrage 08 Pairs and cointegration — Pairs trading 09 PCA residual stat arb — Factor-residual mean reversion 10 Reversal, momentum and costs — Short-term reversal, Momentum 11 Signal transforms and IC D3, D4 — 12 Alpha combination and purged CV F5, V1 — 13 Backtest overfitting: DSR and PBO V4 — 14 Risk model and MVO P1, P2, P3 — 15 Trading toward the aim P6 — 16 Almgren-Chriss frontier E3 — 17 VWAP, TWAP and POV E2, E1 — 18 Smart order router E4 — 19 Trend following and vol targeting P7 Trend following 20 Index reconstitution event study — Flow-driven strategies

docs.title: End-to-end walkthroughs
docs.text:
The capstones. Each follows one business through a full cycle with numbers taken from the labs:

  • A mid-frequency stat-arb book: universe → three alphas → IC-weighted combination → risk model → optimizer with costs → VWAP/IS execution → next-day attribution.
  • A day at an ETF market maker: fair value from basket and futures, quoting, inventory, creation/redemption, hedging, markouts, end-of-day P&L.
  • An options market maker: vol surface → theoretical values → quotes → delta/vega hedging → Greeks P&L attribution.
  • Executing a $500M buy order: schedule choice, child orders, venues, the close, and the TCA report.

docs.title: Algorithm map
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • All 39 algorithm cards on one diagram: five research-to-trading stages (data and signals → forecasting → validation → portfolio construction → execution), a parallel market-making/HFT lane, and live trading as the loop that feeds results back.
  • Every card has a stable ID (D1…L3). The ID's letter tells you the stage; the five canonical pipelines are different paths through the same map.
  • Latency regimes run from nanosecond risk gates to research jobs that take hours. A card's regime tells you what kind of engineering it needs.
  • The map is not a one-way conveyor. Three feedback loops matter: TCA recalibrates the cost model, live monitoring retires decaying alphas, and markouts retune quoting.

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: How to read the map
docs.text: Solid arrows show what feeds what on a normal trading day; dotted arrows show research gates and feedback. Validation cards (V) never touch live orders; they decide whether a forecast reaches production. The market-making lane (M) is a separate, much faster loop that shares venues, risk controls and monitoring with the main pipeline. M9 Algorithmic risk controls sits in that lane, but every live order in every pipeline passes a pre-trade risk check.

  M5 -->|"refit"| M2["M2 Fair value"]
  1. Execution cost loop. TCA feeds realized market impact into the cost model. If impact runs above forecast, the optimizer trades less and schedules slow down. Without it, capacity estimates are guesses.
  2. Alpha lifecycle loop. Attribution splits P&L by signal; decay tests decide when live IC has fallen far enough below the backtest to cut a signal's weight, freeing risk budget for new research.
  3. Adverse-selection loop. Markouts expose adverse selection by venue and counterparty; quoting widens or skews and the fair-value model is refit.
