docs.title: There is no single algorithm
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • "What is their algorithm?" has no one-line answer. A quant firm runs a pipeline: dozens of algorithms, each answering one narrow question. What is the fair price right now? What will this stock do relative to its peers? How much risk is this? How do I buy it without moving the price?
  • The horizon sets the pipeline's shape. A market maker's loop closes in microseconds; a factor fund's closes once a month. A different tempo means a different bottleneck and a different place where money is made or lost.
  • Five canonical pipelines cover most US equity quant trading: the HFT market-making loop, short-horizon stat arb, mid-frequency cross-sectional equity, the systematic factor manager, and agency execution.
  • The edge rarely lives in one clever model. It lives in the joints between stages (forecast and cost model, fair value and quoting) and in unglamorous plumbing: point-in-time data, risk controls, feedback from fills.
  • A better question than "what's your algorithm?" is "which stage of your pipeline is the binding constraint?"

Level: Core · Read time: ~16 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text:
Ask a quant "what's your algorithm?" and you will get a polite non-answer. Secrecy is part of the reason, but mostly the question is malformed. A systematic trading business is a production line of many algorithms, owned by different people, each solving a narrow problem, chained so that one stage's output is the next stage's input. Clean data becomes features; features become forecasts; forecasts become target positions; targets become orders; orders become fills; fills become P&L, which is attributed back to the forecasts that caused it.

A semiconductor fab is the right analogy. Nobody asks a foundry for "its process". They ask about lithography, etch, deposition, metrology and yield, because the product comes out of hundreds of steps and yield is multiplicative. Trading pipelines behave the same way. A forecast with real predictive power can be destroyed by a stale risk model, an optimizer that over-trades, or an execution algo that leaks intent. If each of five stages keeps 85% of what the previous stage delivered, only 44% of the original alpha reaches the P&L (0.85⁵ ≈ 0.44; illustrative).

flowchart LR
  A["Data<br/>D1"] --> B["Signals<br/>D2 D3 D4"]
  B --> C["Forecasts<br/>F1 to F6"]
  C --> D["Portfolio<br/>P1 to P7"]
  D --> E["Orders and fills<br/>E1 to E6, M1 to M9"]
  E --> F["PnL and monitoring<br/>L1 L2 L3"]
  V["Validation<br/>V1 to V4"] -.->|"gates"| C
  F -.->|"feedback"| B

Every pipeline in this KB maps onto these stages, and each stage has its own section of algorithm cards (A to G). The algorithm map puts all 39 cards on one diagram. Businesses differ in tempo and in which stage dominates. Below are the five canonical pipelines for US equities. Each gets a diagram, annotated pseudocode, its latency and compute regime, what dominates its P&L, and the cards used at each stage. The pseudocode is deliberately simplified: one function name stands in for a whole subsystem, and every number in it is illustrative.

docs.title: 1. The HFT / electronic market-maker loop
docs.text:
An electronic market maker continuously posts bids and offers in thousands of symbols. It earns the spread from impatient traders while trying not to be run over by informed ones. Strategies that run this loop: equity market making, ETF market making and options market making. The card-level version of this section is M1 Anatomy of an HFT trading loop.

flowchart LR
  md["Exchange feeds"] --> bb["Book build"]
  bb --> fv["Fair value<br/>M2 M3"]
  fv --> qs["Quote and skew<br/>M4 M6"]
  qs --> rk["Pre-trade risk<br/>M9"]
  rk --> ord["Order to venue"]
  ord --> fil["Fill"]
  fil --> hdg["Hedge<br/>M7"]
  fil --> inv["Inventory update"]
  hdg --> inv
  inv -->|"skew next quote"| qs
  fil -.->|"markouts M5"| fv
Stage What happens Cards Market data → book build Decode each exchange's direct feed; rebuild every venue's book; merge into one view M1 Fair value Mid-price tilted by queue imbalance (microprice), plus order-flow and futures/ETF lead-lag signals M2, M3 Quote and skew Center quotes on a reservation price shifted against inventory; keep or give up queue position M4, M6, M8 for options Pre-trade risk Position, notional, price-collar and message-rate checks before anything leaves M9 Order → fill New / replace / cancel; fills arrive asynchronously E4 for venue choice Hedge Offset unwanted risk in a correlated instrument (futures, ETF, basket, underlying) M7 Inventory and review Update position; measure markouts to detect adverse selection M5, L1 
# Event loop of an electronic market maker for ONE symbol (real systems run thousands in parallel).
# Simplified: production code is C++ or FPGA logic, lock-free and allocation-free. Numbers illustrative.
def on_market_data(msg, s):                        # s = per-symbol state, held in memory
    book = s.book.apply(msg)                       # 1. book build: add / cancel / execute at a level
    fv = microprice(book)                          # 2. fair value: mid tilted toward the thin side (M2)
    fv += s.signals.predict_ticks(book, msg) * s.tick   # + order-flow and futures lead-lag (M3)
    q = s.inventory                                # signed shares
    r = fv - q * s.gamma * s.sigma**2 * s.horizon  # 3. reservation price: long -> shade quotes down (M4)
    half = max(s.min_half_spread, s.half_spread(book, s.toxicity))  # widen when flow is toxic (M5)
    bid = floor_to_tick(r - half, s.tick)
    ask = ceil_to_tick(r + half, s.tick)
    for side, px in (("buy", bid), ("sell", ask)):
        if s.live[side] is not None and s.live[side].px == px:
            continue                               # unchanged price: keep the order and its queue spot (M6)
        o = Order(side, px, size=s.clip_for(side, q))   # smaller size on the side that adds inventory
        if pre_trade_ok(o, s.limits):              # 4. position, notional, collar, rate checks (M9)
            s.gateway.replace(s.live[side], o)     # 5. order out; fills come back asynchronously

def on_fill(fill, s):
    s.inventory += fill.signed_qty                 # 6. inventory update
    s.markouts.track(fill, horizons_s=[0.1, 1, 10])     # adverse-selection monitor (M5)
    h = s.hedger.order_for(fill, s.inventory)      # 7. e.g. offset an ETF fill with futures (M7)
    if h is not None and pre_trade_ok(h, s.limits):
        s.gateway.send(h)

Latency and compute regime. This is the only pipeline where the speed of light and the chip matter. The loop runs in memory on colocated servers. The critical path from an incoming market-data packet to an outgoing order (tick-to-trade) takes microseconds in optimized software and nanoseconds in FPGA hardware. For scale, an FPGA reference design reached a minimum of 13.9 ns in a June 2024 STAC-T0 benchmark [Verified]. That benchmark was vendor-commissioned and measures network I/O only, with no strategy logic. Speed matters because of races. On London Stock Exchange message data, Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill find that the winner of the modal latency-arbitrage race beats the first loser by only 5–10 microseconds, and that about a fifth of FTSE 100 trading volume happens in such races [Verified]. Model fitting (fair-value weights, fill probabilities) happens offline. The live loop evaluates simple, precomputed models because there is no time budget for anything else.

What dominates P&L. Read a market maker's day as an income statement. Revenue is spread capture plus exchange rebates. Cost of goods sold is adverse selection: losses to counterparties who knew more. Below that come inventory gains and losses, then fees and technology. Menkveld's case study of one large HFT market maker in European stocks found gross profit of about €0.88 per trade: €1.55 of spread capture net of fees, less a €0.68 loss on positions [Reported] (working-paper figures). The business runs on the law of large numbers, with a tiny edge per trade and an enormous number of trades. Virtu's 2014 IPO filing reported one losing day in 1,238 [Reported]. Fair-value accuracy, meaning not getting picked off, matters more than cleverness in the quoting formula. The other big lever is cost per message and per fill.

docs.title: 2. Short-horizon stat arb (minutes to days)
docs.text:
A book of hundreds to a few thousand liquid names, usually market- and sector-neutral, rebalanced intraday on forecasts with horizons from about 30 minutes to a few days. Strategies: ML-driven short-horizon alpha, factor-residual mean reversion, short-term reversal and intraday patterns.

flowchart LR
  ft["Features<br/>D1 D2 D3"] --> ml["ML forecasts<br/>F1 F2 F3"]
  ml --> cb["Combination<br/>F5"]
  cb --> op["Optimizer with cost model<br/>P1 P3 P5 P6"]
  op --> ex["Execution<br/>E1 E4 M6"]
  ex --> pos["Positions and PnL<br/>L1"]
  pos -->|"current holdings"| op
  cv["Purged CV and overfitting tests<br/>V1 V4"] -.-> ml
  pos -.->|"realized costs"| op
Stage What happens Cards Features Residual returns, order-flow imbalance, volume surprises, time-of-day effects; identical code in backtest and live D1, D2, D3 ML forecast One model per horizon; regularized linear models and boosted trees are the workhorses F1, F2, F3 Validation Purged, embargoed cross-validation; deflate for the number of trials V1, V4 Combination Blend horizons and models into one expected return per name F5 Optimizer with cost model Trade only where expected alpha beats expected cost; trade partway toward target P1, P3, P5, P6 Execution Passive first, cross the spread when alpha is decaying fast E1, E4, M6 
# Intraday stat-arb rebalance, every 5 minutes over ~2,000 liquid US names (illustrative values)
def rebalance(now, w_now, models, risk, cost, nav):
    X = build_features(now)                     # D2: residual returns, imbalance, volume surprise,
                                                #     time of day; same code path as the backtest
    X = X.apply(winsorize, k=4).apply(zscore)   # D3: cross-sectional scaling, outliers clipped
    preds = {h: m.predict(X) for h, m in models.items()}   # F1/F2: one model per horizon (30m, 2h, 1d)
    alpha = sum(wt * preds[h] for h, wt in HORIZON_WEIGHTS.items())  # F5: weights fit out of sample (V1)
    alpha = neutralize(alpha, risk.exposures)   # strip market, sector and style tilts; units: bps

    # P3 + P5 + P6: maximize alpha'w - risk_aversion * risk(w) - cost(w - w_now)
    w_tgt = optimize(alpha_bps=alpha, risk=risk, w0=w_now,
                     cost=lambda dw: cost.half_spread(dw) + cost.impact(dw),  # square-root impact
                     risk_aversion=5.0, max_name=0.004, max_gross=4.0,
                     dollar_neutral=True)
    trades = (w_tgt - w_now) * nav              # dollars per name
    trades[trades.abs() < 5_000] = 0            # no-trade band: small trades cost more than they earn
    for sym, usd in trades.items():
        urgency = alpha_halflife(sym)           # fast-decaying alpha -> cross the spread sooner
        send_to_execution(sym, usd, urgency)    # E1/E4/M6: passive first, take liquidity if urgent
    return w_tgt

Latency and compute regime. Decisions come every few minutes to an hour, and features update continuously. The optimizer must solve a 1,000–3,000-name problem in seconds. Models retrain offline, nightly or weekly, on CPU or GPU clusters [Estimate] (reasoning: a forecast horizon of 30 minutes or more leaves seconds of slack per decision, not microseconds). Latency matters in the execution leg, because passive orders need decent queue position. It does not matter for the forecast.

What dominates P&L. A tug-of-war between gross alpha and trading costs. At these horizons a good forecast is worth a few basis points per trade, the same order of magnitude as the half-spread plus market impact. An illustrative case: a forecast of +6 bps over two hours on a large-cap with 150 bps daily volatility. The square-root law puts impact at about Y·σ·√(Q/V) [Verified] (Tóth et al.). With Y = 0.7 (illustrative), trading 0.1% of daily volume costs about 3.3 bps of impact; trading 1% costs about 10.5 bps. The same signal makes money in small size and loses money in large size. That is why the cost model and the trade-toward-target logic sit at the center of this pipeline. Turnover is high: an average holding period of one to two days means trading roughly 50–100% of the gross book every day [Estimate] (turnover ≈ 1 / holding period). Signals of this kind also decay. In Avellaneda and Lee's academic backtest, net of their cost assumption, the PCA-residual strategy earned a Sharpe of 1.44 over 1997–2007 in the working draft. The published version reports an average of only 0.9 for 2003–2007 [Verified].

docs.title: 3. Mid-frequency cross-sectional equity (days to weeks)
docs.text:
This is classic quant equity market-neutral. Dozens to hundreds of signals (value, quality, analyst revisions, sentiment, short-term reversal, alternative data) are combined into one forecast per stock. A risk model and an optimizer then turn those forecasts into a neutral book, rebalanced daily. Strategies: cross-sectional alpha and neutralization, fundamental quant signals, analyst revisions and sentiment and alternative data. The mid-frequency walkthrough runs this pipeline end to end with numbers.

flowchart TD
  d["Point-in-time data<br/>D1"] --> a["Alphas<br/>D2 F4"]
  a --> t["Transforms and evaluation<br/>D3 D4"]
  t --> c["Combination<br/>F5 F1"]
  c --> o["Optimizer<br/>P3 P4 P7"]
  rm["Risk model<br/>P1 P2"] --> o
  tc["Cost model<br/>P5"] --> o
  o --> tl["Trade list<br/>P6"]
  tl --> ex["Execution algos<br/>E2 E3 E5"]
  ex --> at["Attribution<br/>L1 E6"]
  at -.->|"retire or reweight"| c
  at -.->|"recalibrate"| tc
Stage What happens Cards Data As-of-date fundamentals, prices, estimates; delisted names kept D1 Alphas Raw signals from prices, fundamentals, text D2, F4 Transforms Winsorize, z-score, industry-neutralize; track information coefficient (IC) and decay D3, D4 Combination IC-weighted or regression blend, shrunk toward equal weights F5, F1 Risk model Factor exposures, factor covariance, specific risk P1, P2 Optimizer → trade list Max alpha minus risk minus cost, subject to neutrality and caps P3, P4, P5, P6, P7 Execution algos VWAP for most names, IS for urgent ones, part at the close E2, E3, E5 Attribution Split P&L into factor, specific, cost and unexplained L1, E6, L2 
# Nightly batch for a market-neutral US equity book (~3,000 names); trades go out tomorrow
def nightly_run(d, positions):
    data = load_point_in_time(d)                 # D1: values as known on date d; delisted names kept
    raw = {k: f(data) for k, f in ALPHAS.items()}     # D2/F4: value, quality, revisions, reversal, text
    sig = {k: neutralize(zscore(winsorize(v, 3.0)), data.industry)   # D3: comparable, industry-neutral
           for k, v in raw.items()}
    ic = {k: rolling_ic(sig[k], data.fwd_ret, window=252) for k in sig}   # D4: live track record
    z = combine(sig, weights=ic_weights(ic, shrink=0.5))   # F5: IC-weighted, shrunk toward equal weight
    alpha = IC_COMBINED * data.resid_vol * z     # Grinold's rule: forecast = IC x volatility x score

    B, F, D = risk_model(data)                   # P1/P2: exposures, factor covariance, specific variance
    w = optimize(alpha, B, F, D, w0=positions,
                 risk_aversion=10.0,
                 tcost=impact_model(data.adv, data.vol),            # P5
                 constraints=[beta_neutral(), industry_net(0.01),   # P3/P7: neutral and capped
                              name_cap(0.01), gross_leverage(4.0)])
    trades = shares(w - positions, data.close)
    trades = trades[trades.abs() >= 100]         # drop trades too small to be worth a ticket
    algos = assign_algos(trades, default="VWAP",              # E2: most of the list
                         urgent="IS", close_frac=0.25)        # E3 for fast alpha, E5 for the close
    return trades, algos

def morning_attribution(d):                      # L1/E6: where did yesterday's P&L come from?
    return decompose_pnl(d, parts=["factor", "specific", "trading_cost", "unexplained"])

Latency and compute regime. Overnight batch. Data land after the close, the pipeline runs in a few hours, and trading happens the next day through VWAP and IS schedules or the closing auction. The heavy compute is in research: thousands of backtests over decades of point-in-time data. Production is light. The optimizer for about 3,000 names with a factor risk model solves in seconds [Estimate]. Reasoning: it is a convex quadratic program with about 3,000 variables, and the covariance is factor-structured rather than a dense 3,000 × 3,000 matrix. MSCI's Barra USE4 model, for example, uses 60 industry factors, 12 style factors and one country factor [Verified].

What dominates P&L. Breadth of many weak signals. The fundamental law of active management (Grinold and Kahn) says the information ratio is roughly IC × √breadth. Take an IC of 0.02 on 2,000 names re-forecast monthly (illustrative). Breadth is 24,000, and the theoretical IR is 0.02 × 155 ≈ 3.1. Three things then cut it down. Bets are correlated. Constraints dilute the signal: the transfer coefficient is often 0.3–0.7 [Estimate]. Costs take a further share. A realized net IR of 1–2 is considered strong [Lore]. In accounting terms, P&L = unintended factor exposure (should be near zero) + stock-specific alpha − trading costs − financing. The risk model's job is to shrink the first term.

docs.title: 4. Systematic factor manager (monthly)
docs.text:
Long-only or long/short portfolios tilted toward documented factors (value, momentum, quality, low volatility), often managed against a benchmark. There are few signals, they are transparent, and capacity is large. Strategies: factor investing fundamentals, momentum, value, quality and low volatility and factor timing and crowding.

flowchart LR
  fs["Factor scores<br/>value, momentum, quality, low vol"] --> pc["Constrained construction<br/>P1 P3 P4 P7"]
  bm["Benchmark and constraints"] --> pc
  pc --> rb["Monthly rebalance<br/>P5 P6"]
  rb --> ex["VWAP or closing auction<br/>E2 E5"]
  ex --> mon["Monitoring<br/>L1 F6"]
  mon -.->|"next month"| fs
  bt["Backtests and overfitting tests<br/>V2 V3 V4"] -.-> fs
Stage What happens Cards Factor scores Point-in-time composites per factor, winsorized and z-scored D1, D3 Research gate Long backtests, multiple-testing discipline V2, V3, V4 Constrained construction Maximize factor exposure within a tracking error budget and position limits P1, P3, P4, P7 Rebalance Turnover caps and no-trade bands; simple cost model P5, P6 Execution and monitoring Multi-day VWAP or the close; regime and exposure monitoring E2, E5, L1, F6 
# Monthly rebalance of a long-only multi-factor fund vs a large-cap benchmark (illustrative values)
def monthly_rebalance(d, holdings, bench):
    univ = universe(d, min_mcap=2e9, min_adv_usd=20e6)          # D1: point-in-time, liquid names only
    s = pd.DataFrame({
        "value":    zscore(book_to_price(univ) + earnings_yield(univ)),
        "momentum": zscore(total_return(univ, months=12, skip=1)),   # 12-1 month momentum
        "quality":  zscore(gross_profitability(univ) - accruals(univ)),
        "low_vol":  zscore(-volatility(univ, days=252)),
    }).clip(-3, 3)                                              # D3: winsorized composites
    score = s.mean(axis=1)                                      # equal weights: hard to overfit
    w = optimize_vs_benchmark(                                  # P3/P4: most exposure per unit of risk
        score, bench=bench, w0=holdings,
        tracking_error=0.03,                                    # ~3% active risk budget
        max_active_name=0.015, max_active_sector=0.03,
        turnover_cap=0.20,                                      # P6: one-way monthly turnover limit
        tcost=linear_cost(bps=8))                               # P5: a simple cost model suffices here
    trades = w - holdings
    trades[trades.abs() < 0.0005] = 0                           # no-trade band: skip < 5 bp changes
    return schedule(trades, algo="VWAP", days=2, close_frac=0.3)    # E2/E5

Latency and compute regime. Rebalancing is monthly or quarterly, often with a no-trade band so that many names go untouched. Production compute is trivial; a single workstation could run it [Estimate]. Academic reference portfolios show the cadence: Fama–French size and value portfolios are re-formed once a year at the end of June, and momentum monthly [Verified]. The engineering effort goes into data history and into trading large rebalances cheaply.

What dominates P&L. The factor premia themselves, which arrive in lumps over years, minus implementation drag: turnover, costs and the dilution forced by tracking-error limits. Multi-year drawdowns come with the territory. Value suffered a deep drawdown in the late 2010s that ended only in late 2020, visible in the HML series of the French Data Library [Reported]; see the failure gallery. Research discipline is the real edge. Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue that so many factors have been tested that a new one should clear a t-statistic of about 3.0, not the usual 2.0 [Verified].

docs.title: 5. Agency execution
docs.text:
A broker's algorithms execute a client's parent order by slicing it into many child orders over time and across venues. Every institutional investor uses this pipeline, and it forms the execution leg of the other four. The institutional execution walkthrough follows a $500M order through it. Related strategy: auctions and closing liquidity.

flowchart LR
  po["Parent order<br/>buy 2M shares"] --> pre["Pre-trade estimate<br/>P5"]
  pre --> sch["Schedule<br/>E2 VWAP or POV, E3 IS"]
  sch --> ch["Child orders<br/>M6 E5"]
  ch --> sor["Smart order router<br/>E4"]
  sor --> lit["Lit exchanges"]
  sor --> drk["Dark pools"]
  sor --> auc["Open or close auction"]
  lit --> tca["TCA<br/>E6"]
  drk --> tca
  auc --> tca
  tca -.->|"recalibrate impact"| pre
Stage What happens Cards Parent order and pre-trade estimate Expected cost and risk for the size, given volume and volatility P5, E1 Schedule Implementation shortfall (front-loaded), VWAP (volume curve) or POV (fixed participation) E2, E3 Child orders Size, price and post-vs-take for each slice; auction and dark tactics M6, E5 Smart order routing Pick venues and order types using fees, fill odds and toxicity E4 TCA Compare fills with arrival, interval VWAP and close; feed the cost model E6 
# Agency execution of one parent order, e.g. BUY 2,000,000 shares by today's close (illustrative)
def execute_parent(order, mkt, cost_model):
    est = cost_model.pretrade(order.qty, adv=mkt.adv, vol=mkt.vol)   # P5: expected impact and risk
    if order.algo == "IS":                                  # E3: Almgren-Chriss, front-loaded
        target = ac_schedule(order.qty, horizon=order.horizon, eta=est.eta,
                             sigma=mkt.vol, risk_aversion=order.urgency)
    elif order.algo == "VWAP":                              # E2: follow the expected volume curve
        target = lambda t: order.qty * mkt.volume_profile.cum(t)
    filled = 0
    for t in mkt.clock(step_seconds=15):
        if order.algo == "POV":                             # E2: fixed share of printed volume
            want = order.rate * mkt.volume_since(order.start)   # e.g. rate = 0.10
        else:
            want = target(t)
        need = min(want, order.qty) - filled
        if need <= 0:
            continue
        if order.limit is not None and mkt.ask(t) > order.limit:
            continue                                        # price guard: never chase blindly
        child = make_child(need, passive_frac=0.6,          # M6: post most, take the rest
                           max_show=mkt.median_trade_size)  # small, unremarkable slices
        for venue, qty, px in smart_route(child, mkt.books(t), fees=mkt.fees):  # E4/E5: lit, dark
            filled += send(venue, qty, px)
    return tca(order, filled, benchmarks=["arrival", "interval_vwap", "close"])  # E6

Latency and compute regime. Mixed. The schedule is computed when the order arrives and re-optimized every few seconds to minutes. The smart order router decides in microseconds to milliseconds. TCA runs after the trade, usually overnight [Estimate].

What dominates P&L. For the client, P&L is cost. Implementation shortfall, in Perold's 1988 definition, is the gap between a paper portfolio traded instantly at the decision price and the real one. It breaks into spread, impact, timing drift and the opportunity cost of shares never filled. Almgren and Chriss framed scheduling as a trade-off: trade slowly to cut impact, or fast to cut exposure to price moves. The result is an efficient frontier of schedules [Verified]. For the broker, revenue is commission, and algo desks compete on TCA league tables. The edge is less impact and less information leakage than rival algos. The cautionary tale is 6 May 2010. A large seller used an algorithm set to 9% of the previous minute's volume, without regard to price or time, to sell 75,000 E-mini futures contracts (about $4.1B). As volume exploded during the crash, the algorithm sold faster [Verified]. In equities, the same failure is a POV order with no limit price.

docs.title: The five pipelines side by side
docs.text:
Pipeline Horizon Decision frequency Where the edge is Hardest engineering problem Typical failure HFT / market-making loop Seconds to minutes of inventory; near flat by the close Every market-data event; microsecond reaction Fair-value accuracy, speed, queue position, cost per message Deterministic low latency across thousands of symbols, with risk checks inline Picked off on stale quotes; runaway order logic (Knight 2012) Short-horizon stat arb 30 minutes to a few days Every few minutes to hourly Many weak, short-lived signals netted against precise cost estimates Identical features in research and production; an accurate cost model Costs overtake decaying alpha; crowded unwinds (August 2007) Mid-frequency cross-sectional Days to weeks Daily, overnight batch Breadth: many signals combined, plus a good risk model and optimizer Point-in-time data and research tooling that resists overfitting Factor crowding, look-ahead bias, unmodeled risk such as short squeezes Systematic factor Months to years Monthly or quarterly Cheap, disciplined harvesting of documented premia at large capacity Trading large rebalances cheaply; turnover control Multi-year factor drawdowns ("quant winter"); crowding Agency execution Minutes to days per order Seconds for the schedule; µs–ms for routing Lower impact and less leakage than rival algos Impact and fill-probability models; venue analysis Price-insensitive schedules in thin markets (May 2010); leakage

Horizons and decision frequencies are typical orders of magnitude, not firm-specific facts [Estimate]. Two failures in the table are documented by regulators. On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital's router generated more than 4 million executions in 154 stocks within 45 minutes, and the firm lost over $460 million [Verified]. Khandani and Lo trace the August 2007 quant losses to rapid unwinding of similar long/short equity portfolios [Verified].

The five pipelines share a spine. Each has a forecast: even an agency algo forecasts volume and short-term price moves. Each has a cost model, a risk limit and a feedback loop from fills back to research. Each also fails in the same quiet way when the research version of a stage drifts from the live version. Since 2011, US broker-dealers with market access must run automated pre-trade risk controls under SEC Rule 15c3-5 [Verified]. That is why a risk gate appears in every live pipeline, not only the fast one.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: "Which stage of your pipeline takes most of your research time?" The answer tells you where they believe their edge is.
  2. Basic: "What's the horizon of your main forecasts, and how often do you rebalance?" This places them among the five pipelines in one sentence.
  3. Informed: "How do you guarantee that features in the backtest are computed exactly as in production?" Research-to-live drift is the most common silent killer.
  4. Informed: "Is your cost model calibrated on your own fills, and how often is it refit?" This tests whether the TCA → cost model feedback loop actually exists.
  5. Informed: "When the optimizer refuses to trade a strong signal, how do you tell whether the risk model or the cost model is responsible?" This shows whether they debug at the joints between stages.
  6. Sharp: "What fraction of gross alpha survives to net P&L, and which stage leaks the most?" 🔒
  7. Sharp: "What's your transfer coefficient after constraints?" 🔒
  8. Sharp, market making: "How do one-second markouts differ by venue and counterparty type, and what does the quoting logic do when they deteriorate?" 🔒
  9. Sharp: "What test retires a signal, and how many did you retire last year?" 🔒

docs.title: Alpha decay detection and model retirement
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Alphas decay through publication, crowding, capacity and market-structure change. Across 97 published predictors, returns fell ~26% out of sample and ~58% after publication (McLean & Pontiff 2016).
  • Telling decay from bad luck is slow: SE(Sharpe) ≈ \(\sqrt{(1 + SR^2/2)/T}\) with SR and \(T\) in the same units, about \(1/\sqrt{\text{years}}\) for daily data. Separating Sharpe 1.0 from 0 at two standard errors takes about four years.
  • Monitors stack weak evidence: rolling IC t-stats, a CUSUM alarm on signal P&L, a Bayesian Sharpe posterior, crowding and capacity checks.
  • Retirement is staged (watch, down-weight, freeze, retire), and alarms trigger a human review, not an automatic kill.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: live · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Has this signal stopped working or is it having a bad run, and how much capital should it keep? Inputs → Outputs daily signal P&L and IC, backtest prior, ex-ante risk, crowding and cost data → alarm state, posterior Sharpe, weight multiplier, review ticket Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Fundamental quant signals · Analyst revisions · Alternative data · NLP and LLM signals · ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Short-term reversal · Momentum · Factor timing and crowding Latency / compute regime overnight batch after attribution; milliseconds per signal, minutes for thousands of signals Key parameters backtest haircut 30–60%; prior SD 0.3–0.7 Sharpe; IC window 63–252 days; CUSUM slack \(k\) = half the shift to detect, threshold \(h\) for a 3–5 year false-alarm interval Main failure modes killing good signals at drawdown lows; detecting too late; false alarms across many signals; cost or data errors mistaken for decay Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Think of a goodwill impairment test. A signal was booked at its backtested value; each period, live evidence tests whether the carrying value is impaired. The catch: the evidence is so noisy that one bad year is weak proof, yet waiting for proof means funding a dead signal for years. Good monitors balance the two errors explicitly, like a credit watch list.

docs.title: Where it sits in the pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  att["L1 attribution: signal P&L and IC"] --> mon
  bt["Backtest prior, haircut"] --> mon
  crowd["Crowding and capacity data"] --> mon
  mon["L2 decay monitor"] --> comb["F5 alpha combination weights"]
  mon --> risk["P7 risk budget"]
  mon --> rev["Research review: refit, fix or retire"]
  rev --> res["New research and validation V1-V4"]
  style mon fill:#ffd54f,stroke:#333

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Each night take the signal's standalone P&L and its information coefficient from attribution.
  2. Rolling IC t-stat over 63–252 days: mean IC ÷ (SD of IC ÷ √n). Below 2 is not significant; persistently below 1 puts the signal on watch.
  3. CUSUM (Page 1954) on standardized P&L shortfall: \(S_t = \max(0, S_{t-1} - z_t - k)\); alarm when \(S_t > h\). It accumulates only persistent underperformance and forgets isolated bad days.
  4. Bayesian Sharpe: shrink the live Sharpe ratio toward a haircut prior, weighting each by its precision.
  5. Diagnose the cause: crowding, capacity (costs rising with AUM), or publication.
  6. Act: posterior ÷ prior scales the weight the combiner gives the signal; alarms open a review.
import numpy as np

def decay_monitor(daily_pnl, daily_ic, vol_daily, sr_prior=1.0, prior_sd=0.5,
                  shift_sr=1.0, h=25.0, ic_window=126):
    """Nightly decay monitor for one signal (arrays, one entry per day).
    daily_pnl: standalone signal P&L from attribution; vol_daily: ex-ante daily P&L sigma
    sr_prior: annual Sharpe believed at launch, already haircut from the backtest
    shift_sr: Sharpe drop we want to catch (1.0 = alpha gone)
    h: CUSUM threshold in daily-sigma units (25 ~ one false alarm per 5 years)"""
    mu0 = sr_prior * vol_daily / np.sqrt(252)        # expected daily P&L if alpha is intact
    k = 0.5 * shift_sr / np.sqrt(252)                # slack = half the shift, in sigma units
    S, rows = 0.0, []
    for t in range(len(daily_pnl)):
        z = (daily_pnl[t] - mu0) / vol_daily         # standardized surprise vs expectation
        S = max(0.0, S - z - k)                      # lower CUSUM: grows on persistent shortfall
        alarm = S > h

        ic = daily_ic[max(0, t - ic_window + 1): t + 1]
        ic_t = ic.mean() / (ic.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(ic))) if len(ic) > 20 else np.nan

        n = t + 1                                    # Bayesian update of the annual Sharpe
        sr_hat = np.mean(daily_pnl[:n]) / vol_daily * np.sqrt(252)
        se2 = (1 + (sr_hat / np.sqrt(252)) ** 2 / 2) * 252 / n   # Lo (2002), iid, annualized
        w = (1 / prior_sd**2) / (1 / prior_sd**2 + 1 / se2)       # weight on the prior
        sr_post = w * sr_prior + (1 - w) * sr_hat

        weight_mult = float(np.clip(sr_post / sr_prior, 0.0, 1.0))  # sent to the combiner
        rows.append((t, S, alarm, ic_t, sr_post, weight_mult))
        if alarm:
            S = 0.0                                  # human review opens; restart the count
    return rows

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
How long until a drop is statistically visible? With daily data, SE(annual Sharpe) ≈ \(\sqrt{1/T}\) for \(T\) years. A two-standard-error gap needs \(T = (2/\Delta SR)^2\):

Sharpe before → after Drop Years to a 2-SE gap 1.0 → 0 1.0 (2/1)² = 4.0 3.0 → 1.5 1.5 (2/1.5)² = 1.8 8.0 → 4.0 4.0 (2/4)² = 0.25 (≈ 3 months)

The absolute drop is what matters, so a high-Sharpe market maker sees decay in weeks while a monthly factor book needs years.

Bayesian update (illustrative). Prior N(1.0, 0.5²), so prior precision 4. One live year at Sharpe −0.2 has variance ≈ 1/1 (precision 1): posterior = (4 × 1.0 + 1 × −0.2) ÷ 5 = 0.76. Two such years (precision 2): (4 − 0.4) ÷ 6 = 0.60. Three: (4 − 0.6) ÷ 7 = 0.49. The weight multiplier falls to 0.76, 0.60, 0.49.

CUSUM, \(k\) = 0.5/√252 = 0.0315, \(h\) = 25. A −1.5σ day adds 1.5 + 0.063 − 0.0315 ≈ 1.53 to \(S\). In 300 simulated Gaussian paths per case [Estimate]: mean time to a false alarm with Sharpe intact ≈ 5.1 years; mean time to alarm after Sharpe falls to 0 ≈ 1.6 years, to −0.5 ≈ 1.2 years, to 0.5 ≈ 2.7 years.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Prior haircut: start from a backtest Sharpe cut by 30–60%, in line with the out-of-sample evidence below [Estimate].
  • Threshold \(h\): set from the false-alarm interval you can afford. With 200 signals and one false alarm per signal per 5 years, expect ~40 reviews a year [Estimate], which is why alarms open reviews instead of killing signals.
  • Stages (illustrative): watch on alarm or IC t-stat below 1; down-weight by posterior ÷ prior; freeze capital below 0.5; retire after a review finds no economic story.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Live
  Live --> Watch: CUSUM alarm or IC t below 1
  Watch --> Live: review finds noise
  Watch --> DownWeighted: posterior below prior
  DownWeighted --> Frozen: posterior below half of prior
  Frozen --> Retired: no economic story
  Frozen --> Live: new evidence, re-validated
  Retired --> [*]

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Publication decay: McLean & Pontiff (2016) find returns of 97 predictors fall ~26% out of sample (an upper bound on data mining) and ~58% post-publication, so at least ~32% (58 − 26) reflects publication-informed trading [Verified].
  • Out-of-sample decay: Falck, Rej & Thesmar (2022) find 72 published strategies keep about half their in-sample performance; publication date predicts decay best, and overfitting proxies add roughly 15% explanatory power [Verified].
  • Crowding: Lou & Polk's comomentum (excess return correlation among momentum stocks) flags crowding; when high, momentum returns tend to revert [Verified]. Desks also watch short interest in the short leg and holdings overlap [Lore].
  • Capacity decay is yours alone: gross alpha holds, net falls as impact rises with size (cost models) [Estimate]. Plot gross and net bps against AUM.
  • Textbook: test "Sharpe = 0". Practice: tests lack power, so firms shrink and down-weight gradually [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Realized false-alarm rate matches the designed interval.
  • Retired signals, paper-traded afterwards, earn about zero; if they keep earning, the monitor is too trigger-happy [Lore].
  • Posterior Sharpe predicts next year's realized Sharpe better than the backtest does.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Pro-cyclical retirement: killing a factor at the bottom of a crowding drawdown locks in the loss (quant winters).
  • Regime vs decay: a signal dormant in one regime looks dead.
  • Autocorrelated P&L (overlapping holding periods) shrinks the true sample; use effective \(T\).
  • Re-launching variants of a retired idea is multiple testing in disguise (V4).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "It's in the penalty box." → down-weighted pending review.
  • "Is that decay or a drawdown?" → structural loss or bad luck?
  • "CUSUM tripped on the revisions sleeve." → persistent shortfall alarm fired.
  • "Comomentum is spiking." → crowded trade; unwind risk rising.
  • "The alpha's fine; we're too big for it." → capacity decay.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. What haircut do you apply to backtest Sharpe before going live?
  2. How many years of live data before you trust a signal's Sharpe?
  3. Do alarms trigger automatic de-risking or a review?
  4. How do you separate capacity decay from alpha decay?
  5. 🔒 Which crowding indicators actually led your drawdowns?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: Sharpe standard error, Bayesian update, CUSUM run lengths

For iid returns, per-period Sharpe \(s\), \(n\) periods (Lo 2002):

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat s) \approx \frac{1 + s^2/2}{n}. \]

With \(q\) periods a year (\(n = qT\)): \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{SR}) \approx (1 + SR^2/2q)/T\); for daily data the \(SR^2\) term is negligible. Fat tails and autocorrelation raise it (Bailey & López de Prado 2012).

Prior \(N(\mu_0, \tau^2)\), estimate variance \(\sigma^2/T\):

\[ \mu_{\text{post}} = \frac{\mu_0/\tau^2 + \widehat{SR}\,T/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2 + T/\sigma^2}. \]

A standard approximation for Gaussian CUSUM (\(b = h + 1.166\)) gives mean run length \((e^{2kb} - 2kb - 1)/2k^2\) ≈ 1,285 days here, matching the simulation.

docs.title: Live monitoring and P&L attribution
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Attribution splits P&L into lines with an owner and an expected value: factor vs specific (alpha), holding vs trading, cost vs the cost model, and each alpha sleeve's share.
  • Quant equity book: P&L = Σ (dollar factor exposure × factor return) + specific P&L + trading P&L. Alpha should appear in the specific line.
  • Market maker: the same idea as an income statement: spread capture + rebates − adverse selection ± inventory − hedging costs − fees.
  • Monitoring adds exposures, limits, fill rates, latency and drift, wired to alerts someone acts on.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: live · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Did the book make money for the reasons the model says, and is anything drifting or about to break? Inputs → Outputs positions, fills, prices, risk-model exposures and factor returns, cost forecasts, sleeve targets → P&L by factor, specific, trading, cost and sleeve; dashboards and alerts Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Retail flow internalization · Cross-sectional alpha · Factor-residual mean reversion · ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Stat arb overview Latency / compute regime real time for marks and limits (sub-second at a market maker); end-of-day batch attribution (seconds for 3,000 names × 60–80 factors) Key parameters risk model (≈ 10 styles + 50–70 industries); markout horizons 1 s–5 min; alert bands (P&L beyond 3σ of ex-ante risk, slippage > 1.5–2× model, limit usage > 80%) Main failure modes bad marks; attribution model ≠ optimizer's; naive sleeve splits; ignored alerts Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Think segment reporting plus budget-vs-actual variance analysis. Each line has a budget: specific return P&L should be positive on average (the alpha), factor P&L near zero in a neutral book, costs close to the cost model. The variance says where to look: beta, a style tilt, stock picks or the trading itself.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Reconcile. P&L from positions and cash must match the books to the dollar; a residual is a data problem.
  2. Holding P&L = prior-close dollars × today's return: the no-trade P&L.
  3. Factor split. With \(r_i = \sum_k X_{ik} f_k + u_i\) from the risk model, dollar factor exposure \(E_k = \sum_i h_i X_{ik}\) earns \(E_k f_k\); the rest, \(\sum_i h_i u_i\), is specific P&L.
  4. Trading P&L = total − holding. Split into slippage vs arrival (implementation shortfall) and post-arrival drift; compare slippage with the model.
  5. Per-alpha. Run each sleeve's paper portfolio through steps 2–4; the gap to the real book is a netting line.
  6. Link days so monthly lines still sum; alert on lines outside their bands.
import numpy as np

def factor_attribution(h_start, h_end, px_prev, px_close, fills, X, f, model_cost_bps):
    """One day's attribution for an equity book; all money in $.
    h_start, h_end: shares at prior close / today's close, shape (N,)
    fills: list of (i, signed_shares, fill_px, arrival_px)
    X: (N, K) risk-model exposures; f: (K,) today's factor returns
    model_cost_bps: (N,) pre-trade cost forecast. Fees, rebates, borrow booked separately."""
    r = px_close / px_prev - 1.0                     # total stock returns
    dollars = h_start * px_prev                      # $ held at the start of the day
    holding_pnl = dollars * r                        # P&L had we not traded

    exposure = X.T @ dollars                         # $ exposure per factor, (K,)
    factor_pnl = exposure * f                        # P&L per factor, (K,)
    u = r - X @ f                                    # specific (residual) returns
    specific_pnl = dollars * u                       # per-stock alpha P&L, (N,)

    trading, slip, slip_model = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for i, q, fill_px, arrival_px in fills:
        trading += q * (px_close[i] - fill_px)       # fill marked to the close
        slip += -q * (fill_px - arrival_px)          # vs arrival; negative = cost
        slip_model += -abs(q) * arrival_px * model_cost_bps[i] / 1e4

    total = holding_pnl.sum() + trading
    cash_spent = sum(q * p for _, q, p, _ in fills)
    books = h_end @ px_close - h_start @ px_prev - cash_spent
    assert abs(total - books) < 1e-6 * max(1.0, abs(books)), "unexplained P&L: fix data"
    return {
        "factor": factor_pnl,                        # should be ~0 on average if neutral
        "specific": specific_pnl.sum(),              # the alpha line
        "trading": trading,
        "slippage_vs_arrival": slip,
        "slippage_vs_model": slip - slip_model,      # > 0: cheaper than the model said
        "after_arrival_drift": trading - slip,       # timing, not execution quality
        "total": total,
    }

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. One factor (beta). Long $10M of A (beta 1.2), short $10M of B (beta 0.8). Factor return −2.0%; A returns −1.5%, B −3.0%.

  • Dollar beta 10 × 1.2 − 10 × 0.8 = +\(4M → factor P&L = **−\)80,000**.
  • \(u_A\) = −1.5% + 2.4% = +0.9% → +$90,000; \(u_B\) = −3.0% + 1.6% = −1.4%, short earns +\(140,000 → specific **+\)230,000**.
  • Holding: −$150,000 + \(300,000 = +\)150,000 = −80,000 + 230,000 ✓.

The book also bought 50,000 A: arrival $99.80, average fill $99.86, close $98.50.

  • Trading P&L = 50,000 × (98.50 − 99.86) = −$68,000.
  • Slippage vs arrival = −50,000 × 0.06 = −\(3,000 (6 bps); the model said 8 bps (−\)3,992), so execution beat it by $992.
  • The other −$65,000 is A falling after arrival: a timing question, not execution.

Total +$82,000. The alpha made $230,000; an unintended beta tilt cost $80,000. Fix the hedge, not the alpha.

A market maker's day as an income statement:

Line $ (illustrative) Measured as Spread capture +120,000 signed qty × (mid at fill − fill price) Rebates net of take fees +35,000 fee schedule × volume Adverse selection −85,000 markout: qty × (mid +1 min − mid at fill) Inventory P&L −10,000 drift beyond the markout horizon Hedging costs −15,000 hedge slippage and fees Clearing and regulatory fees −8,000 per share and notional Net trading income +37,000

Watch adverse selection ÷ spread capture (here 71%).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Risk model: use the optimizer's, or "factor P&L" stops meaning "risk we chose or failed to hedge".
  • Markout horizons: 1 s, 10 s, 1 min, 5 min; the curve's shape matters more than one point (M5).
  • Alert bands: scale to ex-ante risk; warn near 80% of a limit, hard stop at 100% [Lore].
  • Dashboards: factor and sector exposures, limit usage, fill rates, order-to-ack latency (p50/p99), live vs training forecast distribution (drift), each with an owner.
flowchart TD
  m1["Metric breaches band"] --> a1{"Hard limit?"}
  a1 -->|yes| k1["Automatic block or kill switch"]
  a1 -->|no| p1["Page the strategy owner"]
  p1 --> r1{"Explained within 15 min?"}
  r1 -->|no| e1["Escalate to risk desk, cut size"]
  r1 -->|yes| l1["Log cause, tune band"]

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: Brinson sector attribution vs a benchmark. Practice: factor attribution off the risk model; vendor tools report factor contributions, specific return and trading impact [Verified] (MSCI).
  • Holding vs trading is Perold's paper-vs-real portfolio gap (1988) [Verified].
  • Linking: daily lines do not sum to compounded returns; Menchero (2004) finds one linking method meets all his criteria [Verified].
  • Market makers: Menkveld's study of one HFT market maker found ≈ €1.55 per trade of spread capture net of fees against ≈ €0.68 of positioning losses [Verified] (working-paper figures).
  • Monitoring: before Knight Capital's 2012 loss, 97 automated emails flagged an error pre-open, but were not designed as alerts and went unread; the SEC's first market access rule case followed ($12M penalty) [Verified].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Reconciliation residual is zero daily.
  • Factor P&L averages near zero in a neutral book; a persistent sign is an unhedged bet.
  • Realized ÷ forecast slippage ≈ 1.0 over 20 days (TCA).
  • Daily P&L ÷ ex-ante σ has standard deviation 0.8–1.2 [Estimate]; otherwise suspect the risk model.
  • Specific-P&L Sharpe tracks the haircut backtest; slides go to alpha decay detection.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Bad marks: stale closes or missed splits book phantom specific P&L.
  • Leakage: an alpha with a momentum tilt shows as factor P&L; hedging it away hedges away alpha.
  • Pro-rata sleeves: sleeves wanting +\(6M and −\)2M; pro-rating the +$4M net misstates both.
  • Alert fatigue: amber lights train people to ignore red ones.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Specific was +2.3 bps; we gave it back on beta." → the alpha worked, the hedge didn't.
  • "What's the unexplained?" → reconciliation residual; nonzero means bad data.
  • "Slippage ran 1.4× model." → costs above forecast.
  • "Markouts go negative at ten seconds." → informed flow is picking us off.
  • "Momentum ate us on the attribution." → a style factor dominated.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Is your attribution model the optimizer's risk model?
  2. What share of P&L variance is factor vs specific?
  3. How do you split P&L across alphas in a netted book?
  4. Which alert last fired, and what changed afterwards?
  5. 🔒 What markout horizon defines "toxic" for you?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: factor attribution and the market-maker identity

Holdings \(h\) (dollars), exposures \(X\), regression factor returns \(f\):

\[ h^\top r = (X^\top h)^\top f + h^\top u . \]

One fill of signed size \(q\) at price \(p\); mid \(m_t\) at fill, \(m_{t+\tau}\) at the markout horizon, \(m_T\) at the close:

\[ q(m_T - p) = \underbrace{q(m_t - p)}_{\text{spread}} + \underbrace{q(m_{t+\tau} - m_t)}_{\text{adverse sel.}} + \underbrace{q(m_T - m_{t+\tau})}_{\text{inventory}} . \]

Cost is \(O(NK)\) per day.

docs.title: Reinforcement learning in trading
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Reinforcement learning (RL) learns a policy (state → action) that maximizes cumulative reward when today's action changes tomorrow's state. Execution, market making and hedging fit because inventory carries over.
  • Key evidence: Nevmyvaka, Feng & Kearns (2006) on execution, Spooner et al. (2018) on market making, Buehler et al. (2019) on deep hedging. Most results beat simple baselines, not production algos.
  • Hard because markets are non-stationary, simulators cannot show how the market reacts to you, agents exploit simulator flaws, and there is one history to learn from.
  • Reported production use is mainly bank execution (J.P. Morgan's LOXM, 2017); deep hedging came from J.P. Morgan researchers. RL as a quant-fund profit engine is lore.

Level: Deep dive · Pipeline stage: live · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which actions (trade size, quote placement, hedge size) maximize reward when each action changes the next state? Inputs → Outputs state features (time left, inventory, spread, imbalance), a simulator or replay, a reward → a policy (table or network), tested against model-based baselines Used by strategies Equity market making · Options market making · ML-driven short-horizon alpha Latency / compute regime training offline (CPU-hours to GPU-days); inference µs–ms (table lookup or small network); decisions every 1–60 s for execution Key parameters discount γ 1.0 (finite-horizon execution) to 0.99–0.999 (market making); learning rate 0.01–0.1; exploration ε 0.05–0.2, decaying; 5–20 buckets per state variable; inventory or risk penalty; 10⁴–10⁷ episodes Main failure modes overfitting the simulator; reward hacking; regime change; costly live exploration; opaque policies Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Supervised learning predicts; RL decides. A price forecast does not say how fast to sell 10,000 shares, because selling moves the price and what you still hold shapes the next choice. That is dynamic programming, as in real-options valuation, except RL learns the transitions by trial and error. The problem is framed as a Markov decision process:

Problem State Action Reward Baseline to beat Execution time left, shares left, spread, imbalance child size or limit-price offset −slippage vs arrival mid × shares; penalty for leftovers TWAP, Almgren-Chriss Market making inventory, spread, microprice signal, volatility bid and ask offsets, size spread P&L + inventory mark − inventory penalty Avellaneda-Stoikov quotes Hedging position Greeks, time to expiry, cost hedge trade size −risk measure of hedging error − costs delta hedge with bands

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
Tabular Q-learning for a toy liquidation:

  1. Discretize state: step \(t\) and lots left.
  2. Keep a table \(Q(s, a)\): total reward expected from action \(a\) in state \(s\), then acting well.
  3. Each step, mostly take the best-looking action, sometimes a random one (ε-greedy exploration).
  4. Observe reward \(r\) and next state \(s'\); nudge \(Q(s,a)\) toward \(r + \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\).
  5. Repeat for many episodes; the greedy policy is the argmax of each row.
import numpy as np

def q_learning_execution(n_lots=10, lot=1_000, T=5, max_sell=4, half_spread=0.01,
                         eta=1e-6, sigma=0.10, risk_aversion=2e-5,
                         alpha=0.1, eps=0.1, n_episodes=50_000, seed=0):
    """Tabular Q-learning: sell n_lots * lot shares within T steps.
    State = (step t, lots left); action = lots to sell now (0..max_sell).
    Reward = -(half-spread + linear temporary impact) - variance penalty on unsold shares.
    Simplified: price noise enters only via the risk penalty, so rewards are
    deterministic; a real study replays historical order books instead."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Q = np.zeros((T + 1, n_lots + 1, max_sell + 1))   # Q[t, lots_left, action]

    def step(t, inv, a):
        a = inv if t == T - 1 else min(a, inv)        # last step: must sell what is left
        q = a * lot                                   # shares sold now
        cost = q * (half_spread + eta * q)            # spread + impact ($)
        risk = risk_aversion * ((inv - a) * lot * sigma) ** 2   # $ penalty for holding risk
        return -(cost + risk), inv - a

    for _ in range(n_episodes):
        inv = n_lots
        for t in range(T):
            if inv == 0:
                break
            explore = rng.random() < eps              # epsilon-greedy exploration
            a = int(rng.integers(max_sell + 1)) if explore else int(Q[t, inv].argmax())
            r, nxt = step(t, inv, a)
            target = r + (Q[t + 1, nxt].max() if nxt > 0 else 0.0)  # gamma = 1
            Q[t, inv, a] += alpha * (target - Q[t, inv, a])         # TD update
            inv = nxt
    return Q, Q.argmax(axis=2)                        # policy: lots to sell per (t, lots_left)

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Sell 10,000 shares in 5 steps; half-spread $0.01; impact $0.001 per 1,000 shares sold in a step; σ = $0.10 per share per step; risk aversion 2 × 10⁻⁵ per dollar.

  • All at once: 10,000 × (0.01 + 0.01) = $200, no risk penalty.
  • TWAP (2,000 per step): cost 5 × 2,000 × 0.012 = $120; risk 2 × 10⁻⁵ × (800² + 600² + 400² + 200²) = \(24; total **\)144**.
  • Learned 4-2-2-1-1 (thousands): cost 56 + 24 + 24 + 11 + 11 = $126; risk 2 × 10⁻⁵ × (600² + 400² + 200² + 100²) = \(11.4; total **\)137.4**, the brute-force optimum.

One update by hand: from \(Q = 0\), selling 4 lots at \(t=0\) gives \(r\) = −(56 + 2 × 10⁻⁵ × 600²) = −63.2; next-state values are still 0, so \(Q\) ← 0 + 0.1 × (−63.2 − 0) = −6.32. After convergence that entry reaches −137.4, the full cost-to-go.

The toy front-loads, as Almgren-Chriss does in closed form. RL earns its keep only when the state carries information the closed form ignores, such as spread and imbalance.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Reward design matters most: raw P&L teaches the agent to gamble on inventory; add inventory and leftover penalties.
  • State size: 10 variables × 10 buckets is 10¹⁰ cells, so real work uses function approximation (tile coding, neural networks).
  • Data split by time, with the test period after training, as in time-series cross-validation.
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Agent
  participant M as Market or simulator
  A->>M: action (sell 4 lots)
  M-->>A: reward (minus cost and risk)
  M-->>A: next state (t=1, 6 lots left)
  A->>A: update Q toward reward plus best next value

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Execution: Nevmyvaka, Feng & Kearns used 1.5 years of millisecond NASDAQ order-book data (12 months train, 6 test); state was time and inventory left plus market variables, action the limit price; they report substantial gains over baselines [Verified], roughly 27–36% over submit-and-leave per a course summary [Reported]. Ning, Lin & Jaimungal's double deep Q-network beat TWAP on most of nine stocks [Verified].
  • Market making: Spooner et al.'s temporal-difference agent, trained in a limit-order-book simulator with a reward shaped to control inventory risk, beat simple benchmarks and an online-learning method [Verified].
  • Hedging: Buehler et al.'s deep hedging minimizes a convex risk measure and beat the complete-market hedge under transaction costs in a Heston model; two authors were at J.P. Morgan [Verified].
  • Production: the FT reported in 2017 that J.P. Morgan's LOXM used deep RL trained on historic and simulated trades in European equity algos, constrained while it learned; performance claims are the bank's [Reported]. RL quoting at HFT firms has no public evidence [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• It beats the model-based baseline out of sample, after costs, with confidence intervals.
  • The policy is sane: sells faster with more inventory and less time; skews quotes against inventory.
  • Simulated fill rates and slippage match shadow trading; a gap means the simulator is being gamed.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Simulator fidelity: replayed history cannot react to your orders. Agent-based simulators such as ABIDES try to [Verified], but calibration is hard.
  • Reward hacking: agents find simulator artifacts, e.g. assuming a fill whenever price touches the order [Lore].
  • Non-stationarity: tick sizes, fees and competitors change; old policies degrade (alpha decay).
  • Sample efficiency: one history; a daily policy sees 252 decisions a year, and live exploration costs real money.

For the wider literature, see the survey by Hambly, Xu & Yang (2023) [Verified].

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "It's just DP with a learned model." → RL as approximate dynamic programming.
  • "What's the reward?" → the first question; most bugs live there.
  • "It learned the simulator, not the market." → overfit to simulator artifacts.
  • "Does it beat Almgren-Chriss net of costs?" → the right baseline.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Which baseline does it beat, by how many bps out of sample?
  2. Replay or agent-based simulation? How is impact modeled?
  3. Did the agent ever game the reward?
  4. What triggers retraining?
  5. 🔒 Which decisions in your stack are learned policies vs closed-form rules?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: Bellman equation, Q-learning, deep hedging objective

Optimal action values satisfy

\[ Q^*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}\left[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \mid s, a\right], \]

which Q-learning approximates stochastically; tabular memory is \(O(|S||A|)\).

Deep hedging chooses hedge ratios \(\delta_t\) from a network to minimize a convex risk measure \(\rho\) of the hedged payoff \(Z\):

\[ \min_{\delta} \; \rho\left(-Z + \sum_t \delta_t (S_{t+1} - S_t) - C_T(\delta)\right), \]

with \(C_T\) the transaction costs.
